true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Two `def self.downsize` definitions silently shadow each other

Lines 145 and 149 both define `def self.downsize(...)`. Ruby does not support method overloading; the second definition (line 149) replaces the first (line 145). Any existing caller that previously invoked `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` will now dispatch to the new method, with the integer `max_width` being interpreted as a pre-formatted dimensions string and `max_height` being put inside the opts hash. This silently breaks every existing caller of the 4-argument form, and the now-redundant definition on line 145 should be removed (or renamed) before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check is hardcoded to 10MB and ignores site settings

validateUploadedFile now uses `var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024;` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. Client-side validation no longer reflects the site's configured upload limit and loses the per-type `max_image_size_kb` / `max_attachment_size_kb` distinction. If a site admin configures a different limit, users will be blocked from uploading files the server would accept, or allowed to upload files the server rejects.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated-GIF downsize path passes an invalid dimensions value to gifsicle

When SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is true, OptimizedImage.optimize routes through downsize_instructions_animated, which builds `gifsicle ... --resize-fit #{dimensions} ...`. The controller passes the literal string `"80%"` as dimensions, but gifsicle's `--resize-fit` flag expects pixel dimensions of the form `WxH`, not a percentage. The animated-GIF auto-downsize path will fail or resize to nonsensical dimensions, defeating the feature for the very case the SiteSetting is meant to support.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 entity-too-large error message hardcodes 10MB regardless of the real server limit

The case-413 branch now shows the user `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` irrespective of the actual server-side cap. When the server's effective limit differs from 10MB (because max_image_size_kb or the new download cap has been reconfigured), the error dialog misreports the threshold the user must satisfy. The user-facing message is now decoupled from the server's real limit.

Auto-downsize gate uses filename extension instead of actual content type

The new block is gated on `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`. For URL-sourced uploads the filename is derived from `File.basename(URI.parse(url).path)`, which frequently does not reflect the actual response (e.g., a JPEG served as `download.bin` or `attachment`). Real images with non-image filenames will skip auto-downsize and may exceed the configured limit, while non-image files masquerading as `.jpg` will be piped through OptimizedImage.downsize and likely corrupted by ImageMagick before being persisted.

Auto-downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value and proceeds even on total failure

The while loop re-checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` but never inspects the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. OptimizedImage.convert_with rescues every error and returns false on failure (e.g., ImageMagick not installed, corrupt source), but the controller discards that signal and only decrements `attempt`. If all five iterations fail, the upload proceeds with a file that may still exceed the configured limit — or be empty/corrupt from the failed in-place rewrite — and the user receives no indication that auto-resize failed.

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with the same path for input and output

The auto-downsize loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...). The underlying convert (or gifsicle, for animated GIFs) command then opens the file for reading and writing at the same path. ImageMagick and gifsicle will truncate the destination before reading from it, which can produce an empty or corrupt output file. The next call to Upload.create_for will then persist a zero-byte or garbled image with no error surfaced to the caller or user.

URL download size cap is hardcoded to 10MB instead of using the site setting

FileHelper.download is now called with `10.megabytes` instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. The download cap is no longer configurable via the same knob as the rest of the upload flow, and any site whose configured `max_image_size_kb` differs from 10MB will see inconsistent behaviour between direct uploads and URL-sourced fetches. Given the new auto-downsize feature is supposed to let images larger than `max_image_size_kb` through, the download cap should be raised above that setting (or made explicit), not silently frozen at 10MB.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes when host is nil

The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')`. If `host` is nil (which happens when the API receives a request without a host param, or when the record is built in tests without a host), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil`. The callback should guard with `return unless host.present?` or use non-bang `sub` and assign back.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update action crashes when host id not found

`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns nil for an unknown id. The code then calls `save_host(host)`, which executes `host.host = ...` on nil, raising `NoMethodError` and returning a 500. The controller should return 404 (e.g. `raise Discourse::NotFound` or `render status: 404`) when the lookup fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
category_fabricator.rb contains the wrong fabricator

The diff swapped the contents: `category_fabricator.rb` now defines only `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the category fabricators were moved into `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. Although Fabricator looks up by symbol so the tests will run, this is confusing and fragile: anyone reading the file will think it fabricates categories, and any test that needs both will pull from the wrong file. The two files should be swapped back so each filename matches its contents.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in migration via string interpolation

The migration interpolates the host value directly into SQL: `execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)"`. The `h` value comes from splitting the `embeddable_hosts` site setting, which an admin can populate. A value containing a single quote (e.g. `evil.com'); DROP TABLE embeddable_hosts; --`) will break out of the string and execute arbitrary SQL. Use parameterized queries or at minimum escape the value (e.g. `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

false_positives.candidate:
Category referenced only by id, never re-hydrated in client store

EmbeddingSerializer declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, embed: :ids`, and EmbeddableHostSerializer exposes only `category_id`. The Ember side hydrates `category_id` into a `category` object only when the response has `__rest_serializer: "1"` and a `categories` collection in the root. `EmbeddingController#show` passes `rest_serializer: true` but does not include a `categories` collection, so `category` may be undefined on the client even though the controller template renders `{{category-badge host.category}}`. Verify the categories collection is included in the embedding payload, or have the client fetch the category separately.

Combined @on and @observes decorators on same method

`_focusOnInput` is decorated with both `@on('didInsertElement')` and `@observes('editing')`. The `@observes` decorator registers the method as a property observer, while `@on('didInsertElement')` registers it as a one-shot insert listener. Using both is redundant and fragile across Ember versions; the observer semantics differ from the event-listener semantics, and the focus call may not run when expected (or may run when not expected). Use only `@observes('editing')` or only `@on('didInsertElement')`.

Controller spec has no coverage of create/update/destroy

The only assertion is `expect(Admin::EmbeddableHostsController < Admin::AdminController).to eq(true)`. There is no test exercising the create, update, or destroy actions, the `ensure_staff` before filter, the SQL-injection-prone `host.host = params[:...]` mass-assignment, or the not-found path. Given the bugs in those actions (nil host on update/destroy), a regression here would not be caught.

Embedding controller spec has no coverage of show/update

Same as the embeddable_hosts controller: only a parent-class check. No tests verify the serialized payload, staff enforcement, or the `fetch_embedding` ordering.

Missing index on embeddable_hosts.host

The migration creates the `embeddable_hosts` table with a `host` column but no index. `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` runs `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` on every embed request. As the table grows, this will become a sequential scan. Add `add_index :embeddable_hosts, :host` (or a unique index to also prevent duplicate hosts).

Removal of SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host? breaks plugins/clients

The `allows_embeddable_host?` class method was deleted in this PR. Any plugin, theme, or external integration that called it (it is a public class method on a widely used model) will get `NoMethodError` after upgrade. If the goal is to migrate to the new model, keep a deprecated shim that delegates to `EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?` for at least one release cycle.

Uncategorized fallback is silently forced for blank category_id

`host.category_id = SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id if host.category_id.blank?` overwrites an explicitly blank choice with the uncategorized bucket, which may not be what the admin intended. If `SiteSetting.allow_uncategorized_topics` is false (and an admin chose none), this still creates a host pointing at the uncategorized category and the embedded topic will be rejected by the topic validation. Should reject the request with a validation error instead, or require a non-blank category.

deleteHost action passed as a string

The template passes `deleteHost="deleteHost"` (a quoted string) to the component. In Ember this is a literal string, not a reference to the controller's action. The component's `sendAction('deleteHost', host)` will fail to find the action and the host will not be removed from the list after deletion. The attribute should be `deleteHost=(action "deleteHost")` or the equivalent binding that resolves to the controller action.

destroy action crashes when host id not found

`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can be nil, but `host.destroy` is then called on nil, raising `NoMethodError` and producing a 500. Should return 404 when the host doesn't exist.

expandable_first_post? no longer requires any embeddable hosts

The old check `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts.present? && SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?` was replaced with `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`. Since `embeddable_hosts` was removed as a site setting, the check now passes whenever `embed_truncate?` is true and there's a topic embed, even if no embeddable hosts exist in the new `embeddable_hosts` table. The method should check `EmbeddableHost.any?` (or equivalent) to preserve the original semantic that embedding is only expandable when at least one host is configured.

resources :embeddable_hosts exposes undefined show and index actions

`resources :embeddable_hosts, constraints: AdminConstraint.new` generates index, show, create, update, and destroy routes. The controller implements only create, update, and destroy. Requests to GET /admin/embeddable_hosts or GET /admin/embeddable_hosts/:id will hit `index`/`show` and raise `ActionController::UrlGenerationError` or `UnknownAction`. Either add `only: [:create, :update, :destroy]` to the route or implement the missing actions.

saveChanges action is unreachable

`saveChanges` is defined on the controller but no UI element in `embedding.hbs` triggers it (only `addHost` is wired to a button). The corresponding PUT /admin/customize/embedding route and `update` action in `EmbeddingController` are also unused. Either remove the dead code or add a Save button to the template.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`NoMethodError` 500 when the user has no `TopicUser` row

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns `nil` whenever the recipient of the email has never actually visited the topic (for example they were only `@mentioned` or quoted). The very next line does `tu.notification_level > ...`, which raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass` and the user gets a 500 page in place of the intended unsubscribe. The action must handle the no-row case (e.g. via `TopicUser.change`, which already creates the row when missing), or at minimum guard the comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo `stopNotificiationsText` is misspelled

The new controller property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra `i` before `ations`). It is referenced with the same spelling from `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` so it happens to work, but the name should be `stopNotificationsText`. Rename both occurrences to match the locale key (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`) and remove the future risk of someone 'fixing' only one side.

false_positives.candidate:
Action renders the topic page instead of acknowledging the unsubscribe

After mutating the notification level, the action falls through to `perform_show_response`, which renders the normal topic view. The user (who came from an email expecting a confirmation) is dropped on the regular topic page with no visible feedback that anything happened, and the URL they bookmark/share contains `/unsubscribe`. There is no redirect to a confirmation screen and no flash/notice. Either render a dedicated confirmation view or redirect to a stable page that reflects the new state.

Bypassing `TopicUser.change` skips the `MessageBus` publish and reason tracking

`TopicUser.change` is the existing canonical way to mutate a `TopicUser` row: it sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` when `notification_level` changes, publishes `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` so other tabs/clients update in real time, and creates the row when missing. This controller fetches the row, mutates the attribute, and calls `save!`, so (a) no `MessageBus` event is fired (open clients keep showing the old level), (b) `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not refreshed, and (c) any race where the row is deleted between `find_by` and `save!` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. The action should delegate to `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`.

GET request mutates user state, bypassing CSRF protection

The new `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) but it mutates state (changes `TopicUser#notification_level` and calls `save!`). Rails only checks CSRF tokens for non-GET requests, so any third-party page, image, link prefetch, or email preview that causes a logged-in user to issue a GET to these URLs will silently change that user's notification level. By contrast the existing `set_notifications` endpoint in this same controller correctly uses `post`. This new action must be POST/DELETE (or use a signed one-time token) and use Rails' `protect_from_forgery`/`verify_authenticity_token` flow.

No tests cover the new per-topic unsubscribe URL in the email body

The new `unsubscribe_link` server locale adds a `%{unsubscribe_url}` markdown link (`To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})`), and `user_notifications.rb` now passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. The updated spec only asserts that the existing `user_preferences_url` is present; there is no expectation that the new `unsubscribe_url` is actually rendered into the body, nor any test for `Topic#unsubscribe_url`, `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, or the `notification_level` change behaviour. Add a test that the body contains the topic unsubscribe URL and that `Topic#unsubscribe_url` returns the expected path.

Toggle logic downgrades watching/tracking only to `regular`, so the user keeps getting emails

The branch `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` sets the level to `:regular` (which still sends notifications) for users who were `:watching` or `:tracking`. The only path that actually stops emails is the `else` branch (regular/muted -> muted). Users who were actively watching the topic and click 'unsubscribe' will continue receiving notification emails, which is the opposite of what the link promises. The action should mute (or apply the level chosen by the user via the page UI) rather than treat the operation as a `>= regular ? regular : muted` toggle.

`bottom: initial` is unlikely to do what was intended

The new rule `.topic-unsubscribe .notification-options .dropdown-menu { bottom: initial; }` uses the CSS-wide keyword `initial`, resetting `bottom` to its initial value (i.e. `auto`). That just undoes any prior offset and is almost certainly not the intent — the goal was presumably to override the default dropdown placement for the embedded button on the unsubscribe page. Use an explicit value (`auto`, `100%`, or a measured offset) instead of `initial`, otherwise the rule is effectively a no-op.

`ensure_logged_in` makes the email unsubscribe link unusable

The whole point of this feature is the link the user receives in a notification email. The new `:unsubscribe` action is added to the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` list and the route is a plain GET, so any recipient who clicks the unsubscribe link from their mail client without an active Discourse session is bounced to the login page instead of being unsubscribed. Standard email one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058) requires an authenticated-by-token flow; here the URL must carry a per-user, per-topic signed secret that authorises the notification change without requiring a login.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count and last_match_at are written twice per signup because validation runs twice

EmailValidator.validate_each delegates to `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which mutates the database (match_count, last_match_at). UsersController#create does `user.valid? && ... if user.save ...`, so the full validation suite — including this validator — runs once for the explicit `valid?` call and again when `save` re-runs validations. Each invocation of `should_block?` increments match_count by 1, so a single signup attempt with a blocked email inflates the counter by 2 (and any retry, double-click, or page-refresh multiplies it further). Make the validator purely read-only and push the statistics into an `after_validation` callback on User (gated by `email_changed?`), or detect a single increment via `update_all` and short-circuit the second call with an instance flag. Keeping validators free of side effects is the standard Rails contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive; case variants bypass the block

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive equality match, and the migration adds a case-sensitive unique index on the same column. User#email is not downcased on assignment, so a user registering as `Bad@Spam.com` will not match a blocked record stored as `bad@spam.com`, and admins can even create duplicate block rows with different casings. The whole purpose of the feature (stop spammers with known addresses) is defeated by trivial case mutation. Normalize on both sides: store the blocked email in a canonical (lower) form via a `before_validation` callback and add a unique index that ignores case (e.g., a functional index on `lower(email)` or a citext column), and compare with `where('lower(email) = ?', email.to_s.downcase)`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch; whitelist and blacklist are untested

EmailValidator#validate_each has three independent branches (whitelist, blacklist, BlockedEmail) but the spec only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts on the blocked-email path. There is no test that an email matching `email_domains_whitelist` passes, an email outside the whitelist fails with `user.email.not_allowed`, an email matching `email_domains_blacklist` fails, that the two settings do not interact unexpectedly when both are set, or that a nil/blank value is tolerated. Regressions in any of those branches — including the `elsif` ordering that means a non-empty whitelist silently disables the blacklist — will go undetected.

Spec asserts a single increment that production does not produce

The shared example `when a BlockedEmail record matches` calls `subject` once (which calls `should_block?` once) and asserts `match_count` changes by exactly 1. In production `should_block?` is invoked from `User#valid?` and again from `User#save`, so the same signup attempt actually increments by 2. The test passes because it bypasses the validator and exercises the model method directly, masking the doubled-write bug. Add a test that mirrors the controller path (build a User with a blocked email, call `valid?` then `save`, and assert the resulting `match_count`) so the inflated-count issue is caught at the spec level.

rejectedEmails.contains compares strictly, so the user can bypass with a case change

In `emailValidation`, `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` is a strict equality check. The list is populated from `result.values.email`, which is whatever the server stored (case preserved). If the server previously rejected `Bad@Spam.com`, the user simply retypes `bad@spam.com` and the client-side check passes, even though the backend has the same case-sensitivity bug as `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. Lowercase both the stored and compared values (e.g., store `result.values.email.toLowerCase()` and compare `email.toLowerCase()` against the list) so client-side rejection matches the address the user is currently typing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match, allowing spoofed origins

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any event whose origin contains `discourseUrl` as a substring. Anything like `https://attacker.com/?x=https://discourse.host`, or any subdomain/hostname that embeds the literal, passes the check, and the parent's height (or anything else e.data ever carries) can be set by an attacker frame. Because this same message handler also reads any e.data.type, a malicious frame could trigger other branches later. Use `new URL(discourseUrl).origin` (with a trailing slash check) and compare exactly: `new URL(e.origin).origin === expectedOrigin`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported posts created with skip_validations: true and raw_html can persist arbitrary content with no Sanitize pass

When `TopicEmbed.import` creates the initial post it passes `skip_validations: true` along with `cook_method: raw_html`. Combined, the post's `cooked` field stores whatever HTML the caller supplied, including `<script>`, `onerror=`, `<iframe>`, javascript: links, etc., and Post#cook then returns that raw content unmolested. Even though `absolutize_urls` runs on the content, it does not sanitize. Two follow-up problems: (1) the Disqus thor path later creates further reply posts via PostCreator without setting `cook_method`, mixing modes in the same topic; (2) `revisor.revise!(... , skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` overwrites the post with whatever the next import produces, also bypassed. Sanitize imported HTML before storing it and do not pair `skip_validations` with raw_html.

New cook_method column default of 1 likely marks every existing post as raw_html

The migration adds `cook_method integer default 1 not null` to posts. Post.cook_methods is `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` and Post#cook short-circuits to `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. With conventional (0-indexed) Enum implementations `[:regular] == 0` and `[:raw_html] == 1`, so existing rows default to raw_html, which means Post#cook now returns the unprocessed markdown source. The before_save hook does `self.cooked = cook(raw, topic_id: topic_id) unless new_record?`, so the next edit on any existing post will overwrite `cooked` with raw markdown and visibly break rendering across the entire site. The migration default should be whichever value Enum maps to `:regular` (verify the Enum implementation; it is almost certainly 0, not 1).

Stored XSS: untrusted RSS content stored with raw_html cook_method

poll_feed reads `i.content` from the feed, runs only `CGI.unescapeHTML(...scrub)` (which strips invalid bytes but does not sanitize HTML), and passes it straight into `TopicEmbed.import`. import then creates a post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and, because Post#cook returns `raw` for that mode and best.html.erb renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, any `<script>` (or other active) tags in the feed end up executing inside an iframe whose origin is Discourse. The same vector exists for TopicEmbed.import_remote (Readability output is trusted and the raw URL body for Disqus) and the disqus.thor import. Anyone with admin control of feed_polling_url (or embeddable_host, or a Disqus import file) can get script execution in Discourse's origin and read cookies / take actions on behalf of logged-in users visiting the embed iframe. The fix is to never assign raw_html to imported posts from external sources; run them through the normal cook/sanitize pipeline.

Synchronously executes the scheduled PollFeed job on every retrieve

Combined with the fact that the cursor's `value` is also attacker-controlled, this exposes data the cursor protocol was specifically designed to forbid (the existing path in BasePaginator clamps to `max(0, offset)` for forward paging and validates offsets elsewhere). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for any negative start index, so this path can never produce results. The cursor string is parsed by `Cursor.from_string` via `int(bits[1])`, which happily accepts a negative value, so any client (or a hand-crafted cursor) can trigger the crash. Combined with the `organization_auditlogs.py` change that always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, the new admin endpoint is a guaranteed `AssertionError` whenever the resulting cursor has offset < 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misleading 'Performance optimization' comment for a behavior change

The change in `BasePaginator.get_result` from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` is a small behavioral fix, not a performance optimization. The new `max(0, offset)` call is essentially free and does not reduce query cost; it just prevents an `AssertionError` for negative non-prev cursors. The inline comment 'Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets...' is misleading and should describe the actual change (clamping negative non-prev offsets to 0 to avoid a crash). Also note the asymmetry: prev cursors are NOT clamped, so a negative prev cursor will still crash in Django — the two branches should behave consistently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Admin-only pagination branch wraps a broken paginator behind an undocumented query flag

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` enables `OptimizedCursorPaginator` for superusers/org members with global access. Because the paginator's only distinguishing behavior (negative offsets) crashes Django (see paginator.py finding), the branch serves no purpose other than to expose a new failure mode. There is no test in this PR for the new branch, no documentation/changelog entry, and no consumer that actually needs negative offsets. This is dead/unsafe code shipped under an unrelated PR title; it should be reverted from this PR and either fixed properly or removed.

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path

Tests under `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` and `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py` only ever add ~4 spans per segment. The new Lua eviction kicks in at >1000 spans, which is now the actual hard cap on segment size (the Python `max_segment_spans` check was removed), yet nothing exercises it. A test that ingests >1000 spans into one segment is needed to assert: (a) eviction actually happens, (b) the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved, (c) a metric is emitted so the silent-drop path is observable. Without this, regressions in the eviction behavior would land silently.

OptimizedCursorPaginator has no working behavior beyond BasePaginator

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class duplicates almost all of `BasePaginator.get_result` and the only behavior change is the negative-offset branch. Because that branch cannot work (Django rejects negative slicing, see other finding), `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is functionally identical to `BasePaginator`. The `enable_advanced_features=True` flag exposed via `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` therefore does nothing useful in production. The PR title is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'; this entire paginator/auditlog change is unrelated and should be split out. As shipped it adds dead code, a misleading admin-only API knob, and a guaranteed crash path.

Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000, breaking deep segment trees

The loop bound was tightened from 10000 to 1000 while the explanatory comment about depth-10k trees was deleted. The redirect hash chain can still legitimately reach depths above 1000 (the data didn't change), so once `redirect_depth >= 1000` the loop exits early without resolving to a fixed point. The script then writes a `hset` mapping this span's id to an unresolved intermediate `set_span_id` and unions it into the wrong set, so subsequent children of the segment will land in a different buffer key. Result: spans get split across multiple `span-buf:s:*` keys instead of being joined into one segment — segments will be flushed incomplete or duplicated, directly causing data loss/duplication. The previous bound (and its comment) should be preserved unless the maximum possible redirect depth has been proven to be bounded below 1000.

Required `end_timestamp_precise` field added to Span NamedTuple is a contract break

`Span` is a public NamedTuple. Adding `end_timestamp_precise: float` before the defaulted `is_segment_span: bool = False` makes it a required positional argument and breaks every existing `Span(...)` call site that does not supply it (TypeError). All in-repo callers in this PR are updated, but there are likely other consumers (snuba-spans ingestion, tests outside this PR, downstream internal tools) that construct `Span` instances directly. Any such caller will now crash at module/import time on first use, and any older serialized payload that doesn't carry `end_timestamp_precise` will now KeyError inside `process_batch`. This change should either default to `0.0`/`None` or have a clearly documented migration; missing-field handling in `process_batch` is not implemented.

Spans are silently evicted at insert time without any metric or log

After merging incoming spans into `set_key`, the script does `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`. There is no `redis.call('incrby', ...)` for a metric, no log, and the corresponding `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Spans are silently dropped from the segment with zero observability. Worse, the eviction is by lowest `end_timestamp_precise` score, which is not necessarily the spans that are safe to drop (a parent span sent late would have a later score than its children and be kept, while a root span sent early could be evicted, leaving the segment without a root and causing it to fall through to the long `span_buffer_timeout_secs` path or be flushed incomplete). The threshold 1000 also does not match `max_segment_spans=1001` configured on `SpansBuffer`. At minimum this needs a counter (e.g. `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.evicted', n)`), a log when eviction occurs, and a guarantee that the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved.

ZADD uses payload bytes as member; duplicate payloads are silently dropped

Switching the segment from `sadd` to `zadd` keeps the same 'member = span.payload (bytes)' model. Sorted sets require unique members, so two spans whose serialized payloads happen to be byte-identical (e.g. retries, duplicate Kafka messages, or same span replayed) will be collapsed to one entry on insertion. The Lua script's eviction then operates on this collapsed set, and the Python `_load_segment_data` will only see one copy. This is the same potential bug `sadd` had (it also dedups by member), but it is now more consequential because the score-based eviction changes ordering. Worth either documenting the assumption (that payloads are unique) or de-duplicating earlier so that eviction counts are meaningful.

ZUNIONSTORE used with destination equal to one of its source keys

`redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and the analogous `set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key` pass `set_key` as both destination and source. While this happens to behave correctly in some single-instance Redis versions (because the source data is gathered before the destination is rewritten), it is not documented as a supported pattern, can produce non-deterministic results across versions, and is a footgun in cluster mode where slot routing must already match. The safer equivalent is: gather members via ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE, then ZADD them to `set_key` (or union into a temp key and RENAME). At minimum this should be commented and pinned against a tested Redis version.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python hash() of a tuple of ints

The cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids))). While CPython's hash of a tuple of ints is deterministic within a given run, the contract relies on an internal implementation detail (the tuple hashing algorithm for nested ints) and produces a signed Python int that is concatenated into the key string. It would be safer and more portable to use an explicit deterministic digest (e.g. hashlib.md5 of the comma-joined sorted ids) so the cache key is stable across Python versions, implementations, and obvious to readers, and so cache busting via invalidate_upsampling_cache is reliable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Aliased count() columns silently bypass upsampling transform

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling matches column_lower == "count()" exactly. Any column with an explicit alias such as "count() as my_count" or even "count() as count" will not match and falls through to the else branch, which appends the original column unchanged. The endpoint code (organization_events_stats.py) now calls this transform on every y-axis column when upsampling is enabled, so a user who aliases their count column (e.g. for a chart with multiple y-axes) will silently get the raw count() while a user with no alias gets the upsampled value. The fix is to detect count() with optional "as <alias>" and replace the function name while preserving the alias, e.g. emit "upsampled_count() as my_count".

Bare except Exception hides AttributeError/TypeError in sample rate extraction

In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling the first try/except wraps a chain of .get() calls on dicts, which never raise. The except Exception block is dead for the intended path but will silently swallow AttributeError or TypeError caused by a malformed normalized_data (e.g. contexts not being a dict). That makes a broken event manifest look like "no sample rate" instead of failing the test loudly. Catch only the specific exception you expect, or drop the try/except entirely around the .get() chain.

Redundant upsampling_enabled alias of should_upsample

Inside _get_event_stats, should_upsample = is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...) is immediately followed by upsampling_enabled = should_upsample and the rest of the function only ever reads upsampling_enabled. The second variable adds no semantic value and makes the code look like the two could diverge. Drop one (preferably upsampling_enabled) and use should_upsample directly. (Noted as style rather than bug because there is no functional impact.)

Tests mock options.get but do not clear the 60s upsampling cache

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (error_upsampling.py) caches the boolean result of the allowlist check for 60 seconds using cache.get/set. The four new tests in test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects etc. patch sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options, but if any earlier test in the same run (or a prior test in this class) has populated the cache for the same organization+projects, the cached True/False is returned without re-running options.get and the mock has no effect. This can cause intermittent failures or false successes. The tests should reset the cache (e.g. via cache.clear() or invalidate_upsampling_cache) in setUp/tearDown before patching options.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling mutates all event types, not just errors

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling is invoked unconditionally inside store_event right after manager.get_data() for every event, and writes normalized_data["sample_rate"] whenever contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate is present. The function does not check the event type, so any transaction, attachment, or other non-error event that happens to carry an error_sampling context (whether by a SDK bug, a test fixture, or a future feature) will have sample_rate injected, potentially affecting other code paths that read sample_rate from those events. Guard the call on the event type being an error, or move the logic into the error-specific normalization path.

invalidate_upsampling_cache has no test coverage

invalidate_upsampling_cache is a public helper intended to be called when the allowlist changes, but no test in test_error_upsampling.py exercises it. Without a test, a future change to the cache key format (e.g. switching away from hash()) will silently break cache invalidation in production. Add a test that populates the cache, calls invalidate_upsampling_cache, and asserts cache.get returns None.

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is not exercised

The main public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (which combines the allowlist check, the 60s cache, and the dataset/query filter) is never tested directly. The test file only covers the private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling). The caching behavior in particular is the riskiest new logic and should have a test that verifies a cache hit short-circuits the allowlist lookup.

topEvents error message changed, breaking API contract

The 400 response for topEvents <= 0 was changed from {"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"} to {"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}. This is a user-visible API contract change. Any client or integration that matches the previous string (e.g. Sentry's own frontend, alert rules, or downstream tooling) will stop recognizing the error. Either keep the original wording or coordinate this with the frontend before merging.

upsampled_count assumes sample_weight is non-NULL for every row

The new upsampled_count SnQL aggregate is implemented as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). SQL/ClickHouse sum() ignores NULL values entirely, so any event in an allowlisted project that lacks sample_weight (e.g. older data, a partial backfill, or a schema mismatch) will be silently dropped from the count. The comment in error_upsampling.py asserts the column exists for all events, but nothing verifies it at query time, and the consequence is wrong downsampled charts that look valid. The aggregate should either coalesce NULLs (assume a weight of 1 for rows without sample_weight, or surface a null result) or the allowlist check should validate that backfill has actually completed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data on feature-flag branch

When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the new branch in `tableResultComponent` renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with hardcoded empty values instead of forwarding the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `eventView`, `fields`, `location`, `fieldAliases`, `fieldHeaderMap`, etc. that are still computed above the conditional. Anyone with this flag on will see completely empty table widgets in their dashboards. The non-flagged branch correctly renders `<StyledSimpleTableChart ... data={result.data} metadata={result.meta} ... />`, so the new code path appears to be an unfinished placeholder that needs to be wired up to the same `result` data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before feature-flag check

The new `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` call is placed before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` gate. Any caller without the feature flag still gets a 404 response, but the analytics event is emitted anyway, so the preprod assemble analytics will be inflated by traffic from orgs/projects that have no access to the feature. The analytics call should be moved after the feature check (and ideally inside the try/else branch that actually enqueues work) so it only counts requests that are processed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition allows backup code to be reused under concurrent requests

After a backup code is matched (line 144), the code nulls the used slot in memory and then awaits a prisma.user.update to persist (lines 148-156). Two concurrent login requests that submit the same backup code will both pass the indexOf check against the same in-memory array before either write hits the DB, and both will be authenticated. The second write then overwrites the first with the same nulled array, so the code remains "consumed" but two sessions are created. Mitigation: do the read/compare/null/write atomically (e.g. via prisma.$transaction with a conditional update that only matches if the code is still present), or perform a single UPDATE that removes the specific code rather than rewriting the whole array.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on unmount

A new object URL is created (line 99) and the previous one is revoked only when another URL is created (line 98). When the modal is closed or the component unmounts, the last backupCodesUrl is never revoked, leaking the underlying Blob for the lifetime of the page. Add a cleanup useEffect that calls URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) on unmount, and also revoke it in resetState() / when the user navigates away from DisplayBackupCodes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code authentication path is not exercised by any test

The e2e file has a TODO at line 12 ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and only verifies UI affordances (download/copy/close). The new security-critical paths added in this PR — backup-code login via next-auth-options.ts, backup-code disable via totp/disable.ts, single-use enforcement of backup codes, and the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes ErrorCode mappings in login.tsx — are not covered. Without these tests, regressions in single-use enforcement, race-condition fixes, or error mapping will go undetected. The author also explicitly ticked the checklist item "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works".

ConfirmPassword "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires two API calls

The ConfirmPassword Continue button is type="submit" and is placed inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209, the button is at line 233-240). Clicking it both runs the onClick handleSetup (which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup) and submits the outer form which calls handleEnable, which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable. Because totpCode is empty at this point, the second call always fails and sets an error message in state, even on a successful setup. The button should be type="button" (or moved outside the outer Form) so that only handleSetup runs.

DisplayQrCode "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires handleEnable API call

The "Continue" button on the QR code step is rendered as type="submit" and lives inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209). Clicking it both runs the onClick (which advances to EnterTotpCode) AND submits the form, invoking handleEnable which immediately calls TwoFactorAuthAPI.enable() with whatever totpCode is currently in the form (empty or stale from a previous attempt). The result is a wasted API round-trip and an error toast like "code is incorrect" being briefly shown to the user before the step transitions. The button should be type="button" since its only intent is to advance the wizard step.

No rate limiting on 2FA disable endpoint, enabling brute-force of TOTP/backup code

The disable handler accepts a TOTP code (6 digits, ~20 bits of entropy) or a backup code (10 hex chars, 40 bits) and attempts verification on every request. Unlike the next-auth credentials authorize (which calls checkRateLimitAndThrowError), this endpoint performs no rate limiting, no lockout, and no failed-attempt counter. A user who is still logged in (or an attacker with a stolen session cookie) can submit unlimited guesses. TOTP is especially vulnerable: 10^6 / 30s is small enough that a targeted attacker can reliably find the current code. Add checkRateLimitAndThrowError (or equivalent) keyed on the user id before running code verification.

Returns 200 success without authenticating when 2FA is not enabled, leaking 2FA status

When user.twoFactorEnabled is false, the endpoint short-circuits with `return res.json({ message: "Two factor disabled" })` (line 37) without ever calling verifyPassword or checking the supplied code. Any caller who knows a valid session can use this to probe whether a given account has 2FA enabled: the response body and status differ from the "needs 2FA / needs password" branches. Either require the same authentication as the 2FA-enabled path before returning, or return a uniform response regardless of 2FA status.

formatBackupCode referenced before declaration; download Blob built on first render

handleSetup (line 77) references formatBackupCode (line 163) inside its body. Because formatBackupCode is a const arrow function declared after handleSetup, this works only via closure hoisting at call time — easy to break by future refactors and confusing to read. More importantly, the Blob on line 95 is built using formatBackupCode but the downloaded file content can drift from what is shown on screen if the formatter changes between setup and download (e.g. different dash placement). Define formatBackupCode before handleSetup (module scope or above the component) so both the display grid (line 204) and the Blob/copy operations (lines 95, 278) use the same definition.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty array on Meet bookings

The new fallback that decides whether to switch the meeting location to Cal Video no longer uses optional chaining. Line 119 destructures `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` into `mainHostDestinationCalendar`, and line 120 reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` directly. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`, `undefined`, or an empty array (a normal state for many bookings), the destructured variable is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`. The previous code (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) safely evaluated to `true` in that case. Any booking whose `location` is Google Meet and that has no destinationCalendar configured will now crash with 500 instead of silently falling back to Cal Video.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Calendar updateEvent passes undefined calendarId when no externalCalendarId is supplied

Inside `updateEvent` the new selection is `selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. The `find` callback compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, but the parent ternary only enters this branch when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (typically `undefined`), so `find` matches nothing and returns `undefined`. The previous code simply used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` and worked for any single-destination booking. As a result, callers like `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (which always omits `externalCalendarId`) now send `calendarId: undefined` to the Google Calendar API, causing the update to 404 even though the destination calendar is present on the event.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Collective events silently drop all host destination calendars when organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized as `null` when neither the event-type nor the organizer user has one (see the `evt = { ... destinationCalendar: ... ? [...] : null }` block around line 1067). The subsequent `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining, so the push becomes a no-op when the value is `null`. As a result, collective bookings that have no event-type-level or organizer-level destination calendar end up with an empty/null `destinationCalendar`, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` falls through to the `cred.type === "calendar"` branch which never matches real credentials (`google_calendar`, etc.). The expected per-host calendar invitations for that scenario are silently lost.

Google Calendar deleteEvent always deletes from "primary" when externalCalendarId is omitted

`deleteEvent` uses the same `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` lookup as `updateEvent`. With `externalCalendarId` undefined (the only form `CalendarManager.deleteEvent` ever calls it with), the lookup never matches and the fallback `calendarId: calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` resolves to `"primary"`. Previously it just used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Bookings whose host's destination calendar is not the user's Google primary calendar will now be deleted from the wrong calendar; for events that don't exist on primary, the 404/410 path silently resolves and the real calendar event is orphaned.

No test covers the core multi-host destinationCalendar fix

The PR author checked the box "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works." The only test change in the whole PR is updating the expected `destinationCalendar` value from `null` to `[]` in `apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts`. There is no integration or unit test exercising the new collective-event path: building the `evt.destinationCalendar` array with organizer + team host destinations, persisting it through `handleNewBooking`, or verifying that `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` fans out to all host calendars. Given the size of the refactor (signatures changed, persistence narrowed, multiple CalendarService adapters updated), this is a significant test gap and the regressions called out above (e.g. TypeError on Meet bookings, dropped team destinations, broken Google update/delete) are likely to pass through CI because nothing in the suite exercises the scenario.

Only the first destination calendar of a collective booking is persisted on the Booking row

When writing the new booking row, the change connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` to the booking's `destinationCalendar` relation: `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. For collective events the array now contains the organizer plus every host's destination calendar (built up by the `teamDestinationCalendars` push on line 1078), but the Booking schema only stores the first entry. Any later code path that consults `booking.destinationCalendar` directly (instead of `booking.references`, e.g. confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts at line ~251, paypal-webhook.ts line 152, deleteCredential.handler.ts line 290) will only see the organizer's calendar and lose information about the other hosts. This contradicts the PR description that the booking now supports multiple destinations per host.

requestReschedule drops user fallback for destinationCalendar (inconsistent with other handlers)

The new assignment is `destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar] : []`. Every other handler in the PR (confirm.handler.ts:175, editLocation.handler.ts:85, handleCancelBooking.ts:251, deleteCredential.handler.ts:290, handleNewBooking.ts:1063) falls back to `user.destinationCalendar` when the booking has none. Here that fallback was removed (it was a typo'd duplicate in the old code), so reschedule webhooks and the reschedule email are now sent with `destinationCalendar: []` even when the booking's owner has a destination calendar configured. This is inconsistent and may mislead recipients about which calendar will be updated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Returns fetch Response object, callers expect axios-style response with .data

When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object instead of calling the refresh function and returning its resolved value. Several integrations then treat the result as the original axios response:

- `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177,192`: does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(...)`. A fetch `Response` has no `expiryDate`; this throws and the token is never saved.
- `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`: does `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. A `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws and the credential update is skipped.
- `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94-96`: does `res?.data` and then `token.access_token`/`token.expiry_date`. With sync enabled `res.data` is `undefined` and the next lines throw.
- `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:84`: passes the `Response` to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>`, which will not produce a `RefreshTokenResp` shape.
- `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:262-264`: passes the `Response` through `handleErrorsJson(response)`; even if it parses, the body will not match `refreshTokenResponseSchema`.

Either the helper should `await refreshFunction()` (i.e. only short-circuit when syncing) or every caller must be updated to consume a `Response`.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
