`updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); }))` does not await the async reminder calls. The handler returns the success response while cancellations are still in flight. Errors from the internal `try/catch` of those helpers are merely logged via `console.log` and the caller never learns if a cancellation failed. Combined with the immediateDelete semantics, a failure means the cancelled booking can still trigger an outgoing workflow reminder. Convert to `await Promise.all(...)` or sequential `for/await`.

Reschedule reminder cancellation not awaited

In `requestReschedule`, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` does not await the async deletion calls. Failures are only logged by the helpers' internal catch and never propagated to the caller, so a SendGrid/Prisma error leaves the reminder in place. Several blocks in the `update` and `delete` mutations (`scheduledReminders.forEach`, `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach`, `remindersFromStep.forEach`, `remindersToUpdate.forEach`, `steps.forEach` calling `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder`) iterate with `forEach` over async functions that are never awaited. Errors from SendGrid/Twilio/Prisma are swallowed inside the helpers' catch blocks. Cancellation loop is sequential

Reminders are cancelled one at a time using `await client.request(...)` inside a `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop. With many reminders to cancel (the whole reason for deferring to a CRON), serializing SendGrid calls slows the CRON. The SendGrid cancel calls are independent, so they can run in parallel via `Promise.allSettled` to keep the request window short and reduce the chance that one slow call blocks the run. The first block deletes every EMAIL reminder with `scheduledDate <= now()` regardless of `cancelled` or `scheduled` state, and the cancellation block runs after. A reminder that was just marked `cancelled=true` while its `scheduledDate` is still in the future (within ~1 hour) is fine, but the unconditional past-date delete means a reminder with `scheduled=false`, `cancelled=true`, and a `scheduledDate` that briefly slipped into the past (e.g., race during reschedule) will be silently deleted before the cancellation CRON ever tries to SendGrid-cancel it. false_positives.candidate:
record_stored_segments now invoked per flusher buffer instead of once on writer

The pre-change code called `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` once per `submit()` on the writer buffer. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()`, which is once per flusher process. With multiple flusher processes this multiplies invocations by N, and crucially drops the call on the actual writer buffer (the original `buffer` argument is no longer stored on `self`). If `record_stored_segments` is a metric emission that tags state, has side effects in Redis, or otherwise isn't idempotent across processes, this is a metric/state regression. Even if it is just a gauge, the cardinality and emission frequency for downstream metrics change.

Dead helper _create_process_for_shard is never called

The newly introduced `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is never invoked anywhere in the module. It is a leftover that duplicates the work of `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` but is unreachable. Leaving dead public-looking methods around risks future callers assuming restart-by-shard works when the mapping actually restarts whole processes.

Killed processes are not joined; replace-by-key can leak zombies

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the old process is killed (when it is a `multiprocessing.Process`) and then immediately replaced in `self.processes[process_index]` by a brand-new process without joining the previous one. The previous process object loses its last reference and becomes a zombie until its finalizer runs. In `join()` the loop calls `process.terminate()` on the still-stored entries but again never joins, leaving zombies for `terminate`d processes. Over many restart cycles this can pile up zombie PIDs and consume resources; combined with the spawn context it is also easy to lose visibility into why flusher processes vanished.

Restart path leaves the previous thread (test mode) running with stale buffer

`_ensure_processes_alive` only kills `multiprocessing.Process` instances; `threading.Thread` instances (created when `produce_to_pipe` is set, e.g. in tests) are explicitly not killed. The new process/thread is then started with a fresh `SpansBuffer`, but the old thread keeps running against its original buffer and continues to call the (now stale) `produce_to_pipe`. In a unit test this can produce phantom messages or assertions against the wrong buffer; in any future deployment that uses threading it would silently leak work. Either always join both kinds, or explicitly document that thread mode is single-shot.

process_restarts accumulates across the lifetime of the consumer

`self.process_restarts[process_index]` is incremented on every unhealthy detection and never reset. Combined with the `>` comparison (which lets the count reach `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 == 11` before raising), any flusher process that crashes 12 times over the consumer's lifetime (including rare, isolated crashes months apart) will permanently take the consumer down with `RuntimeError`. The counter should reset after the process has been healthy for some interval, and the comparison should be `>=` if the intent is exactly `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` restarts.

if not process: continue is dead code

`self.processes[process_index]` is always assigned a `multiprocessing.Process` or `threading.Thread` instance in `_create_process_for_shards`; both are truthy. The `if not process: continue` guard can never fire and should be removed (or replaced with the actual invariant you want to enforce).

Class docstring claims one process per shard but default caps processes at 1

The class docstring now reads 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' But the constructor computes `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, and the new CLI flag `flusher_processes` defaults to 1, so the actual production default is one shared process for all shards. The docstring (and the PR description: 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard') overstates the behavior at default settings. Either reword the docstring/helper text to reflect the 'up to N processes, defaulting to 1' semantics, or change the default to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` to actually deliver 'one process per shard' out of the box.

--flusher-processes help text and default contradict the PR description

The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to `1` and its help string says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says 'let's make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard.' With the default of 1, every shard will be multiplexed onto a single process (because `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` collapses to 1). Operators who read the help text will not realize they have to set `--flusher-processes=<num_shards>` to actually get the documented one-process-per-shard layout. Either set the default to the shard count, or document the trade-off in the option help and in the SpanFlusher docstring.

join() never calls terminate on hung threads and can deadlock the consumer

In `join()`, the wait loop only sleeps until `process.is_alive()` is false or the deadline elapses, and only calls `process.terminate()` for `multiprocessing.Process`. A hung `threading.Thread` (which happens any time `produce_to_pipe` is set) will block `join()` until the deadline. Worse, the loop terminates by calling `process.terminate()` only on the entry currently iterated, with no `process.join()` afterwards; any process that survives past the deadline (e.g. spawn-context process that ignores SIGTERM) will be left as a zombie. Add explicit `join(timeout)` after `terminate()` for both kinds, and a fallback to `_stopped` polling for threads.

test_flusher_processes_limit only checks structure, not correctness of shared-shard flushing

The new test creates 4 partitions, sets `flusher_processes=2`, and only asserts that `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes == 2`, `num_processes == 2`, and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`. It never submits a single message, never produces a KafkaPayload, and never verifies that shards are actually distributed (e.g. that processes share shards correctly, that the buffer the flusher uses is the right one, that segments from every shard eventually flush). The most important behavioral claim of the PR — that multiple shards sharing one flusher process still works — is not tested.

test_backpressure relies on a sleep that is not patched and is likely flaky

`append` uses `sleep` imported via `from time import sleep`, which is a local name bound at import time and is *not* affected by `monkeypatch.setattr('time.sleep', ...)`. So `sleep(1.0)` actually blocks for a real second on each produced payload, while the inner flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` is patched to a no-op. After the 0.1s real sleep, the flusher thread is still blocked inside the very first `append` call and `messages` is empty, so `assert messages` is racing against the producer. The test happens to pass today only because the flusher has not yet produced when the assertion runs, but the assertion is timing-dependent and the comment/help text does not warn about this. Use a sentinel (e.g. set a flag on the first call) instead of sleeping for a wall-clock second, or monkeypatch the local symbol.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

As a result, when the sanitizer splits adjacent text blocks the verifier can still register a spurious difference and incorrectly flag the translation as containing illegal HTML. A regex such as `<!--\s*-->` should be used.

In `verifySafeHtml`, when the English counterpart file cannot be opened, the IOException is caught and rethrown as `new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + englishFile, e)`. The other I/O failure paths in the class surface errors via `MojoExecutionException` (declared on the public `verify` method) so this RuntimeException is inconsistent and bypasses the standard failure reporting of the Maven plugin. Additionally, if a translation is added before its English source lands (e.g. a brand-new locale) the verification will crash instead of skipping or warning. There is also no test for this scenario.

The expression `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` matches any underscore-prefixed locale segment (the inner character class includes `-` and `_` so the suffix can contain hyphens too). It will therefore map, for instance, `messages_zh_TW.properties` to `messages_en.properties` instead of `messages_zh_Hant.properties`/etc., and will silently turn `messages_.properties` into `messages_en.properties`. `, `

`, `

When the English source happens to use uppercase tags, POLICY_NO_HTML is incorrectly selected and the OWASP sanitizer is then forced to make a structural decision that POLICY_SOME_HTML was meant to handle, producing false positives. Because `HTML_TAGS` does not match `<0>` etc., the verifier will select POLICY_NO_HTML for those values, and the OWASP sanitizer (which treats `<0>` as an unknown tag) will strip them, causing the verifier to flag legitimate translations as illegal HTML. Combined with the fact that the cursor's `value` is also attacker-controlled, this exposes data the cursor protocol was specifically designed to forbid (the existing path in BasePaginator clamps to `max(0, offset)` for forward paging and validates offsets elsewhere). The new path must either reject negative offsets outright or bound them to a small, signed window (e.g. `max(-limit, cursor.offset)`).

BasePaginator previously did `queryset[offset:stop]` for both forward and prev pagination. The new code does `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` before slicing, which silently clamps negative offsets to 0 only for forward cursors. The inline comment calls this a "performance optimization for high-traffic scenarios" and asserts "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but this is actually a behavior change, not an optimization: any existing caller that produced a negative offset on a forward (is_prev=False) cursor — including cursors built by _build_prev_values whose is_prev is later overridden, or test fixtures, or cursors from older clients — will now incorrectly restart from the beginning of the dataset instead of returning the intended page. The docstring and commit message should describe it as a behavior change, and the change should be validated against every existing caller before merging.

The diff only adds the comments "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" / "This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets" above the unchanged line `self.offset = int(offset)`. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Finer-grain cache lock lets two callers build the same index concurrently

After this PR, bleveBackend.BuildIndex only takes cacheMu around the final map assignment (`b.cache[key] = idx`); the actual index creation (bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly and the ListIterator walk) runs unlocked. getOrCreateIndex itself has no synchronization, so two concurrent callers with the same NamespacedResource can both observe an empty cache (GetIndex returns nil), both call s.build, each constructs its own bleveIndex (running through the storage ListIterator independently), and then both contend on b.cacheMu — last writer wins. Each caller uses its own freshly built index for its Search/Origin call, so the cache may not reflect what the first caller is actually using, and the second caller's build duplicates work that was just done; if storage changes between the two walks the two indexes can diverge. Add per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of *sync.Mutex keyed by NamespacedResource, or use sync.Map directly) so only one goroutine builds a given index and other callers wait for it to be cached.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection to the final cache assignment allows concurrent callers to build the same expensive index for the same key, duplicating work before the last cache write wins.

false_positives.candidate:
search.init goroutine panics when the events channel is closed

In the goroutine started by search.init, the receive `v := <-events` is not in the comma-ok form, and the loop then unconditionally calls `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)`. The SQL backend closes the events channel via `defer close(stream)` when its poller returns (e.g., when backend.Stop calls cancel and `b.done` closes). After that, every iteration of the for loop receives nil for `v` (zero value of *WrittenEvent), and `s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil)` then dereferences `evt.Type` on a nil receiver, panicking the goroutine. Because the search watch is now started eagerly inside NewResourceServer on every startup, the lifecycle that closes this channel is reached on every shutdown. The receive should be `v, ok := <-events` with `if !ok { return }` so the goroutine terminates cleanly when the backend is torn down.

search.init watch goroutine is not bound to the server's lifecycle

search.init sets `watchctx := context.Background()` and passes it to `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)`, then spawns a goroutine that processes events with this background context. This context is completely independent of the server's cancellable context (`s.ctx`, which server.Stop cancels via s.cancel). Calling server.Stop therefore does not stop the search watch goroutine; it only terminates once the SQL backend itself is torn down (b.cancel) and the poller's defer closes the events channel. Combined with the missing comma-ok on the channel receive (related finding above), the goroutine can panic during shutdown rather than exit cleanly. The watch should be tied to a context derived from s.ctx so server.Stop halts search indexing promptly, and the backend poller should respect that context for cancellation.

Two independent database pollers run for WatchWriteEvents

Both search.init (search.go ~line 203) and server.initWatcher call s.backend.WatchWriteEvents, and the SQL backend starts a separate poller goroutine for each call. Each poller runs `listLatestRVs` plus per-resource `poll` queries against the database every defaultPollingInterval (100ms), producing essentially the same event stream. With both watchers active the backend is doing two full sets of polls for what could be a single shared source. Before this PR these two watchers were also started, but lazily on the first gRPC call; after this PR they are both started eagerly and synchronously inside NewResourceServer, so this 2x DB load is now paid on every startup. Consider having a single backend.WatchWriteEvents source that fans out to the search index and the broadcaster (e.g., a shared channel that searchSupport.handleEvent and the broadcaster both subscribe to).

Postgres branch is skipped instead of fixed in the integration test

The new lines `// TODO - fix this test for postgres` plus `t.Skip(...)` for GRAFANA_TEST_DB == "postgres" hide a real test reliability problem rather than fixing it. Now that NewResourceServer blocks on Init during module server construction, this code path is more sensitive to slow or failing init, which is plausibly contributing to the CI failure (the comment says "Works locally" but not in Drone). A skip only papers over the failure: the postgres path is no longer exercised at all in CI, so future regressions on it will go unnoticed. The TODO should be tracked and the test should actually run for postgres in CI, or the broader problem should be diagnosed (e.g., separate slow init in NewResourceServer from module server startup so the test has a chance to complete).

Any concrete implementation that does not already accept `**kwargs` will also break if a future caller does pass `assignment_source`. Either remove the parameter from the abstract signature until the status-side fix is implemented, or implement and thread the assignment_source through the status path so the cycle is actually closed.

false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded queue with no backpressure can exhaust memory

In FixedQueuePool.__init__, the queues are created as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, making them unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (line 293) calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If a particular group is slow (e.g., a subscription whose handler hangs), all items for that group accumulate in its dedicated queue without limit. Unlike the existing `BatchStep`/`RunTask` strategies, this new strategy provides no backpressure: the main thread keeps fetching from Kafka and calling submit, so memory can grow without bound until the consumer OOMs. The PR description acknowledges that 'there's still a chance of individual items backlogging a queue' but does not bound the queue or block submit when queues are full.

get_committable_offsets iterates O(max_offset) not O(outstanding)

In OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets, the loop `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` iterates over every offset in the numeric range, even those that were never added (e.g., gaps from compaction, filtered payloads, or pre-existing committed offsets). For a partition with min_offset=0 and max_offset=1_000_000 and only a few outstanding offsets, this is ~1 million iterations per call, and the commit loop calls this once per second per partition. It should iterate over the sorted `all_offsets` set (O(k log k) where k is the number of seen offsets) and break on the first outstanding/missing one.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join silently drops timeout argument

`def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None: self.close()` ignores the `timeout` parameter entirely. Arroyo's ProcessingStrategy contract allows callers to pass a join timeout (e.g., during shutdown sequencing). Silently ignoring it means callers cannot bound how long join blocks, and the strategy will always wait the full internal 5.0s for the commit thread plus however long queue_pool.shutdown takes.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown 5s join can drop in-flight work

`worker.join(timeout=5.0)` only waits 5 seconds, and the worker is a daemon so it is killed on process exit. If a `result_processor` call takes longer than 5 seconds (which is exactly the kind of slow item this PR is designed to isolate), the join times out, the daemon thread is abandoned, and any work it was holding is never reported as completed/comitted. The fix is either to use a configurable/longer timeout, to join the strategy's commit thread only after all queues drain (e.g., call `wait_until_empty` first), or to set `immediate=True` on `q.shutdown()` and document the data-loss tradeoff.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong behavior

The test sets `mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception('Processing failed'), None]` and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But OrderedQueueWorker.run catches the exception in the inner `except Exception` and still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in the `finally`, so offset 100 is marked completed. Offset 101 also completes. Both are contiguous, so the commit loop will commit offset 102 (101+1). The assertion as written would fail in the correct behavior, and the assertion is trivially true when `len == 0` regardless of what happened. The test should instead assert the committed offset reflects both completed messages (e.g., `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`) to actually verify the 'errors don't block other commits' intent.

test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown does not verify graceful behavior

The test submits 5 messages and then immediately calls `factory.shutdown()` without waiting for processing, asserting only `factory.queue_pool is None`. This does not verify that the 5 submitted messages are processed before shutdown, that no offsets are lost, or that the shutdown is actually graceful. Combined with the 5s join timeout in FixedQueuePool.shutdown, this test will pass even if shutdown drops all in-flight work.

Kafka integration test depends on private StreamProcessor internals

The test drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. These are private arroyo methods (leading underscore) and are not part of the public API; they can change between arroyo releases without notice, which would silently break this test. It also relies on `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` and creates real Kafka topics in a `requires_kafka` test, so it is expensive and fragile. A more robust integration test would use the public `run()` method or otherwise not depend on underscore-prefixed methods.

Unreachable queue.ShutDown handler in inner try

The inner `try` block in OrderedQueueWorker.run only wraps `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(...)` and `self.result_processor(...)`. `queue.ShutDown` can only be raised by `queue.Queue.get()` or `queue.Queue.put()`, neither of which is called inside this inner try. The `except queue.ShutDown: break` on lines 142-143 is therefore dead code and can be removed (or, if a put call is later added inside the inner try, the comment should explain why).

The cursor string is parsed by `Cursor.from_string` via `int(bits[1])`, which happily accepts a negative value, so any client (or a hand-crafted cursor) can trigger the crash. Combined with the `organization_auditlogs.py` change that always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, the new admin endpoint is a guaranteed `AssertionError` whenever the resulting cursor has offset < 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misleading 'Performance optimization' comment for a behavior change

The change in `BasePaginator.get_result` from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` is a small behavioral fix, not a performance optimization. The new `max(0, offset)` call is essentially free and does not reduce query cost; it just prevents an `AssertionError` for negative non-prev cursors. The inline comment 'Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets...' is misleading and should describe the actual change (clamping negative non-prev offsets to 0 to avoid a crash). Also note the asymmetry: prev cursors are NOT clamped, so a negative prev cursor will still crash in Django — the two branches should behave consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000, breaking deep segment trees

The loop bound was tightened from 10000 to 1000 while the explanatory comment about depth-10k trees was deleted. The redirect hash chain can still legitimately reach depths above 1000 (the data didn't change), so once `redirect_depth >= 1000` the loop exits early without resolving to a fixed point. The script then writes a `hset` mapping this span's id to an unresolved intermediate `set_span_id` and unions it into the wrong set, so subsequent children of the segment will land in a different buffer key. Result: spans get split across multiple `span-buf:s:*` keys instead of being joined into one segment — segments will be flushed incomplete or duplicated, directly causing data loss/duplication. The previous bound (and its comment) should be preserved unless the maximum possible redirect depth has been proven to be bounded below 1000.

Spans are silently evicted at insert time without any metric or log

After merging incoming spans into `set_key`, the script does `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`. There is no `redis.call('incrby', ...)` for a metric, no log, and the corresponding `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Spans are silently dropped from the segment with zero observability. Worse, the eviction is by lowest `end_timestamp_precise` score, which is not necessarily the spans that are safe to drop (a parent span sent late would have a later score than its children and be kept, while a root span sent early could be evicted, leaving the segment without a root and causing it to fall through to the long `span_buffer_timeout_secs` path or be flushed incomplete). The threshold 1000 also does not match `max_segment_spans=1001` configured on `SpansBuffer`. At minimum this needs a counter (e.g. `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.evicted', n)`), a log when eviction occurs, and a guarantee that the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved.

OptimizedCursorPaginator has no working behavior beyond BasePaginator

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class duplicates almost all of `BasePaginator.get_result` and the only behavior change is the negative-offset branch. Because that branch cannot work (Django rejects negative slicing, see other finding), `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is functionally identical to `BasePaginator`. The `enable_advanced_features=True` flag exposed via `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` therefore does nothing useful in production. The PR title is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'; this entire paginator/auditlog change is unrelated and should be split out. As shipped it adds dead code, a misleading admin-only API knob, and a guaranteed crash path.

Required `end_timestamp_precise` field added to Span NamedTuple is a contract break

`Span` is a public NamedTuple. Adding `end_timestamp_precise: float` before the defaulted `is_segment_span: bool = False` makes it a required positional argument and breaks every existing `Span(...)` call site that does not supply it (TypeError). All in-repo callers in this PR are updated, but there are likely other consumers (snuba-spans ingestion, tests outside this PR, downstream internal tools) that construct `Span` instances directly. Any such caller will now crash at module/import time on first use, and any older serialized payload that doesn't carry `end_timestamp_precise` will now KeyError inside `process_batch`. This change should either default to `0.0`/`None` or have a clearly documented migration; missing-field handling in `process_batch` is not implemented.

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path

Tests under `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` and `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py` only ever add ~4 spans per segment. The new Lua eviction kicks in at >1000 spans, which is now the actual hard cap on segment size (the Python `max_segment_spans` check was removed), yet nothing exercises it. A test that ingests >1000 spans into one segment is needed to assert: (a) eviction actually happens, (b) the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved, (c) a metric is emitted so the silent-drop path is observable. Without this, regressions in the eviction behavior would land silently.

ZADD uses payload bytes as member; duplicate payloads are silently dropped

Switching the segment from `sadd` to `zadd` keeps the same 'member = span.payload (bytes)' model. Sorted sets require unique members, so two spans whose serialized payloads happen to be byte-identical (e.g. retries, duplicate Kafka messages, or same span replayed) will be collapsed to one entry on insertion. The Lua script's eviction then operates on this collapsed set, and the Python `_load_segment_data` will only see one copy. This is the same potential bug `sadd` had (it also dedups by member), but it is now more consequential because the score-based eviction changes ordering. Worth either documenting the assumption (that payloads are unique) or de-duplicating earlier so that eviction counts are meaningful.

ZUNIONSTORE used with destination equal to one of its source keys

`redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and the analogous `set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key` pass `set_key` as both destination and source. While this happens to behave correctly in some single-instance Redis versions (because the source data is gathered before the destination is rewritten), it is not documented as a supported pattern, can produce non-deterministic results across versions, and is a footgun in cluster mode where slot routing must already match. The safer equivalent is: gather members via ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE, then ZADD them to `set_key` (or union into a temp key and RENAME). At minimum this should be commented and pinned against a tested Redis version.

Admin-only pagination branch wraps a broken paginator behind an undocumented query flag

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` enables `OptimizedCursorPaginator` for superusers/org members with global access. Because the paginator's only distinguishing behavior (negative offsets) crashes Django (see paginator.py finding), the branch serves no purpose other than to expose a new failure mode. There is no test in this PR for the new branch, no documentation/changelog entry, and no consumer that actually needs negative offsets. This is dead/unsafe code shipped under an unrelated PR title; it should be reverted from this PR and either fixed properly or removed.

Cache key uses Python hash() of a tuple of ints

The cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids))). While CPython's hash of a tuple of ints is deterministic within a given run, the contract relies on an internal implementation detail (the tuple hashing algorithm for nested ints) and produces a signed Python int that is concatenated into the key string. It would be safer and more portable to use an explicit deterministic digest (e.g. hashlib.md5 of the comma-joined sorted ids) so the cache key is stable across Python versions, implementations, and obvious to readers, and so cache busting via invalidate_upsampling_cache is reliable.

Aliased count() columns silently bypass upsampling transform

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling matches column_lower == "count()" exactly. Any column with an explicit alias such as "count() as my_count" or even "count() as count" will not match and falls through to the else branch, which appends the original column unchanged. The endpoint code (organization_events_stats.py) now calls this transform on every y-axis column when upsampling is enabled, so a user who aliases their count column (e.g. for a chart with multiple y-axes) will silently get the raw count() while a user with no alias gets the upsampled value. The fix is to detect count() with optional "as <alias>" and replace the function name while preserving the alias, e.g. emit "upsampled_count() as my_count".

topEvents error message changed, breaking API contract

The 400 response for topEvents <= 0 was changed from {"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"} to {"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}. This is a user-visible API contract change. Any client or integration that matches the previous string (e.g. Sentry's own frontend, alert rules, or downstream tooling) will stop recognizing the error. Either keep the original wording or coordinate this with the frontend before merging.

Tests mock options.get but do not clear the 60s upsampling cache

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (error_upsampling.py) caches the boolean result of the allowlist check for 60 seconds using cache.get/set. The four new tests in test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects etc. patch sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options, but if any earlier test in the same run (or a prior test in this class) has populated the cache for the same organization+projects, the cached True/False is returned without re-running options.get and the mock has no effect. This can cause intermittent failures or false successes. The tests should reset the cache (e.g. via cache.clear() or invalidate_upsampling_cache) in setUp/tearDown before patching options.

upsampled_count assumes sample_weight is non-NULL for every row

The new upsampled_count SnQL aggregate is implemented as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). SQL/ClickHouse sum() ignores NULL values entirely, so any event in an allowlisted project that lacks sample_weight (e.g. older data, a partial backfill, or a schema mismatch) will be silently dropped from the count. The comment in error_upsampling.py asserts the column exists for all events, but nothing verifies it at query time, and the consequence is wrong downsampled charts that look valid. _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling mutates all event types, not just errors

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling is invoked unconditionally inside store_event right after manager.get_data() for every event, and writes normalized_data["sample_rate"] whenever contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate is present. The function does not check the event type, so any transaction, attachment, or other non-error event that happens to carry an error_sampling context (whether by a SDK bug, a test fixture, or a future feature) will have sample_rate injected, potentially affecting other code paths that read sample_rate from those events. Bare except Exception hides AttributeError/TypeError in sample rate extraction

In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling the first try/except wraps a chain of .get() calls on dicts, which never raise. The except Exception block is dead for the intended path but will silently swallow AttributeError or TypeError caused by a malformed normalized_data (e.g. contexts not being a dict). That makes a broken event manifest look like "no sample rate" instead of failing the test loudly. Without a test, a future change to the cache key format (e.g. switching away from hash()) will silently break cache invalidation in production. Add a test that populates the cache, calls invalidate_upsampling_cache, and asserts cache.get returns None.

The main public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (which combines the allowlist check, the 60s cache, and the dataset/query filter) is never tested directly. false_positives.candidate:
Stale denial cache can block legitimate access for up to 30s after a permission grant

The newly introduced permDenialCache is consulted at the very start of Service.Check (lines 116-121) and short-circuits to Allowed=false before the permCache or the database are touched. There is no invalidation tied to permission changes (grants, role/team membership changes, deletions). Once any (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) tuple has produced a deny response, that deny is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) and will be returned for every subsequent request, even if the underlying database now grants the permission. This is a regression introduced by the PR and works against its stated goal of letting users access newly created resources: any prior deny that happened to land in the cache for the same (name, parent) tuple will hold the new permission back for up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry whenever a permission grant or revocation affects the cached tuple, or use a much shorter TTL so the cache behaves as a brief burst guard rather than a 30s negative answer.

No test covers a stale denial cache blocking access after a permission grant

The denial cache can hold a deny entry for up to 30s after a user was last denied for a (name, parent, action) tuple. There is no test that asserts (and therefore no guard against) the regression scenario: a prior deny is cached for the user, but the underlying store now grants the permission, and Service.Check still returns Allowed=false because the denial cache short-circuits before the new fallback-to-DB path. Adding such a test would either confirm the 30s window is acceptable, or catch it if invalidation is later added.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has dead/confusing logic that always returns false

The newly added `enableSqlExpressions` function reads:

```go
func enableSqlExpressions(h *ExpressionQueryReader) bool {
    enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)
    if enabled {
        return false
    }
    return false
}
```

The function unconditionally returns `false` regardless of the feature flag's state. The `enabled` variable and the `if enabled { return false }` branch are dead code (both branches return `false`). This is confusing because:
1. The function name suggests it checks whether SQL expressions should be enabled.
2. A future maintainer is likely to interpret this as buggy logic and "fix" it (e.g. by returning `enabled` or `!enabled`), which could accidentally re-enable the vulnerable code path.
3. The `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` check is functionally meaningless.

For a security hardening PR, the intent should be expressed unambiguously. Either simplify to `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or rename and invert the logic so the dead branches are removed.

The feature is not merely unimplemented; it has been intentionally disabled to mitigate CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI). A user reading the error or a downstream log/alert may conclude the feature was forgotten rather than turned off for security reasons. The message should clearly state that the feature is disabled (e.g. reference the CVE / security release) so that operators and users understand why a previously working dashboard now errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent callers will redundantly re-read the manifest

The function checks the cache under RLock, then re-acquires a write Lock to populate it. However, it does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write Lock. When N goroutines invoke GetWebAssets concurrently while the cache is still nil (typical at server startup), every one of them passes the RLock check, then takes the write Lock sequentially, and each independently reads `assets-manifest.json` from disk and overwrites the global. The expensive I/O — the very reason the cache exists — is repeated N times. After `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` (line 48) and before the `cdn := ""` line, add `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` to make this a correct double-checked locking pattern. Without it, the race detector is silenced but the cache offers no benefit under cold-cache concurrency.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets, which allows concurrent callers to redundantly populate the cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is overwritten with nil on read error, defeating caching for subsequent calls

On line 69 the code unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result` and on line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err`. If `readWebAssetsFromFile` returns an error (network blip, transient I/O failure), `result` is nil and the global cache is overwritten with nil. Because the write Lock is held, every concurrent caller will observe the cleared cache and will each attempt the file read again; any previously cached value is permanently lost even if it was still valid. The assignment should only happen on success, e.g. `if err == nil { entryPointAssetsCache = result }` before the return. (Note: this behavior pre-existed, but the PR is the natural place to fix it now that the variable is properly guarded.)
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the fetch result is unconditionally assigned to entryPointAssetsCache, so a failed fetch returning nil overwrites a previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

This PR explicitly fixes a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, yet no test file is added or modified. There is no existing concurrent test for GetWebAssets that would have caught the original race, and nothing here guards against reintroducing the same race (e.g. by removing the mutex or by reverting to the unlocked read in a future refactor). A short test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines in parallel and runs under `go test -race` would lock the fix in place and exercise the double-checked locking pattern described above.

Return statement is redundant and obscures intent

Line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err` after having just assigned `entryPointAssetsCache = result` on line 69. Both expressions yield the same pointer, but reading the code one must verify that no other goroutine could have changed the global between the assignment and the return. While holding the write Lock this is safe, but the redundancy invites future bugs (e.g. someone removing the mutex thinking the local `result` is the returned value). Simply `return result, err` is clearer and removes the indirection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

This is a normal/expected operational event during routine annotation cleanup, not an error. Logging it at Error level will fire false alerts on error-monitoring systems, pollute error pipelines, and dump the full list of IDs plus the constructed SQL condition into error logs every minute (after the cleanup.go ticker change). It also passes `"err", err` while `err` is always nil at that point (the function has already returned if it was non-nil). It should be `r.log.Info` or `r.log.Debug`, and the misleading `"err", err` key/value should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine debugging or operational information being logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend using Debug or Info instead. The candidate's additional details do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker frequency bumped 10x without justification

The PR is about fixing MySQL deadlocks in the annotation cleanup, but this change moves `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. That makes the entire cleanup routine (and the now-Err-logging annotation cleanup) run ten times as often. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix, multiplies database load unnecessarily, and combined with the Error-level logs above will multiply the false alerts accordingly. If a higher frequency is wanted, it should be a separate change with its own justification (e.g., a new config flag, defaulting to 10m).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute as increasing cleanup execution frequency and database load, and call for justification or performance review. The candidate's additional logging concerns do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Successful cleanup batch logged as Error

`r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)` is emitted on every successful cleanup batch. This logs a normal successful operation at Error level, producing repeated false-positive alerts whenever the cleanup runs. It also passes `"err", y` where `y` is always nil (since this log is reached only after a successful delete). It should be downgraded to `r.log.Info`/`Debug` and the spurious `"err"` field removed.

`r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", ...)` fires at Error level for routine MaxCount-based cleanup. Same problem as the MaxAge path: normal operations are reported as errors, and `"err", err` is always nil at that point. Should be `Info`/`Debug`.

Successful MaxCount cleanup logged as Error

`r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by count", ...)` is emitted on every successful MaxCount cleanup batch. Again, this is a normal success path, not an error. Downgrade to `Info`/`Debug` and remove the spurious `"err", y` field.

Orphan-tag cleanup routine logged as Error

`r.log.Error("Tags to clean", ...)` fires every time `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` is invoked by the cleanup ticker, even when there are zero orphans (`len(ids) == 0`). With the ticker now running every minute (see cleanup.go change), this floods error logs and triggers false alerts during normal operation. Should be `Info`/`Debug`.

Successful orphan-tag cleanup logged as Error

`r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...)` is emitted on every successful orphan-tag cleanup batch. This is a normal success log, not an error. Downgrade to `Info`/`Debug` and drop the always-nil `"err", y` field.

O(n²) string concatenation when building the SQLite inline IN-list

When `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit`, the code builds the IN-list with `values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0]); for _, v := range ids[1:] { values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) }`. Each `fmt.Sprintf` call copies the entire accumulator, so the total work is O(n²). With the newly added test case using a batch size of 32767, this is roughly a billion operations and ~hundreds of MB of garbage per cleanup batch, and it gets worse for any future larger batch sizes. Use `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join`-style construction with a pre-sized buffer) so the build is O(n).

Deadlock fix has no MySQL integration test coverage

The new and renamed tests (`TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp`, `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst`) only exercise SQLite via `db.InitTestDB(t)`. The bug this PR fixes — annotations writes being rejected due to a deadlock with the cleanup job — is MySQL-specific (see referenced issue #64979). Without a MySQL integration test, a future regression in the locking pattern (e.g., re-introducing a subquery-based DELETE inside one transaction) would not be caught. The PR should include (or rely on an existing) MySQL integration test exercising concurrent inserts and the cleanup loop.

Hard-coded SQLite parameter limit (999) ignores SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER in modern SQLite

The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` uses `const sqliteParameterLimit = 999`. SQLite >= 3.32.0 defaults SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER to 32766, and even older builds can be recompiled with higher limits. The new test case is even named "should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0", but the code itself still assumes 999, so for batch sizes between 1000 and 32766 the code unnecessarily takes the slow, O(n²), unsafe (no parameterization) inline path. The limit should be derived from a runtime check or configured, not hard-coded to 999.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are no longer excluded from splitting

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before the `partition(... , query => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` step. `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep queries that contain `$__range` out of the time-split batches (the existing comment even explains that splitting such queries is incorrect because `$__range` would then be resolved against a sub-range). Because `applyTemplateVariables` resolves template variables and global variables (including `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__from`/`$__to`) on the frontend with the FULL time range, the `$__range` token disappears from `expr` before the check runs. The `isQueryWithRangeVariable` predicate then returns false and the query gets partitioned into `normalQueries` and split into 1-day chunks, each chunk receiving the full range baked into the previously-interpolated `$__range`. The result is wrong data: e.g. `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` over a 2-day dashboard range becomes `count_over_time({a="b"}[2d])` applied to a 1-day sub-range. The check needs to run on the original (pre-interpolation) expression, or `$__range` must be excluded from this frontend interpolation.

The comment in `querySupportsSplitting` says `$__range` is "interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange". After this PR the variable is interpolated on the frontend (`datasource.applyTemplateVariables`) with the full timeRange before the splitting decision, so the justification given in the comment no longer matches the code path. If the exclusion is still intended, the comment should be updated to describe the new ordering (check pre-interpolation expr, or skip `$__range` in the interpolation step); otherwise the check should be removed entirely.

`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` on every non-hidden, non-empty target and passes the interpolated list to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`. Each shard group later builds a `subRequest` from these already-interpolated targets and calls `runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...)`. Inside `runSplitQuery`, the new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` re-runs template interpolation on the same queries. The test `'Interpolates queries before running'` codifies this by asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times for a single-target request (1 + 4 shard groups). Beyond the wasted work, if `applyTemplateVariables` is not strictly idempotent (e.g. it touches scopedVars, fires telemetry, mutates caches, or escalates unknown variables to errors) the second pass can change behavior or throw. Either `runSplitQuery` should be told the targets are already interpolated (skip flag / do not re-apply), or `runShardSplitQuery` should defer interpolation to the inner `runSplitQuery` call.

No regression test for $__range queries being excluded from splitting

The new `'Interpolates queries before execution'` test only covers `$__auto` and `$step` interpolation. There is no test asserting that a query containing `$__range` (or `$__range_s`) is still routed into `nonSplittingQueries` and never time-split. Given that this PR moves the `querySupportsSplitting` decision to after interpolation, this is exactly the regression a test should pin down. Without it, the existing exclusion documented by the `querySupportsSplitting` comment can silently break (see the corresponding finding in `querySplitting.ts`).

The action then renders success_json regardless of how many names were actually accepted, so the admin sees success even when every supplied username was invalid. Strip each username before lookup, and either reject the request or include the not-found names in the response so the caller can tell which entries failed.

add_members crashes with NoMethodError when usernames is sent as an array

params.require(:usernames) accepts whatever shape is sent; if a client posts usernames[]=alice&usernames[]=bob (the standard Rails array-param convention), params[:usernames] is an Array. The subsequent usernames.split(",") then raises NoMethodError because Array has no split method, returning a 500 to the caller. Coerce the param to a string before splitting (e.g. Array(params[:usernames]).flatten.join(",")) or return a 400 when the value is not a String.

save error handler throws when the server returns an empty or non-JSON error body

The save action's rejection handler does var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors; with no guard. When the server returns an empty body, an HTML error page from a proxy (502/504), or any non-JSON content, $.parseJSON throws. The throw escapes the rejection handler and surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection, the bootbox alert is never shown, and the failure is invisible to the admin. Wrap the parse in a try/catch (or check that e.responseText is non-empty and parseable) and fall back to a generic message such as I18n.t('generic_error') when parsing fails.

addMembers action carries an unresolved TODO to clear the input

The addMembers action still contains the comment // TODO: should clear the input but does not implement it. After a successful add the user-selector continues to show the just-typed usernames, so an admin who wants to add more members has to manually delete the previously typed list. Either reset this.set('usernames', null) (and the bound input) after the AJAX call resolves, or remove the TODO comment.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count and last_match_at are written twice per signup because validation runs twice

EmailValidator.validate_each delegates to `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which mutates the database (match_count, last_match_at). UsersController#create does `user.valid? && ... if user.save ...`, so the full validation suite — including this validator — runs once for the explicit `valid?` call and again when `save` re-runs validations. Each invocation of `should_block?` increments match_count by 1, so a single signup attempt with a blocked email inflates the counter by 2 (and any retry, double-click, or page-refresh multiplies it further). Make the validator purely read-only and push the statistics into an `after_validation` callback on User (gated by `email_changed?`), or detect a single increment via `update_all` and short-circuit the second call with an instance flag. Keeping validators free of side effects is the standard Rails contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the email-blocking predicate mutates statistics during what should be a read-only check. The candidate emphasizes repeated validation inflating counters rather than race conditions or misleading naming, but the root concern is the same side effect.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive; case variants bypass the block

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive equality match, and the migration adds a case-sensitive unique index on the same column. User#email is not downcased on assignment, so a user registering as `Bad@Spam.com` will not match a blocked record stored as `bad@spam.com`, and admins can even create duplicate block rows with different casings. The whole purpose of the feature (stop spammers with known addresses) is defeated by trivial case mutation. Normalize on both sides: store the blocked email in a canonical (lower) form via a `before_validation` callback and add a unique index that ignores case (e.g., a functional index on `lower(email)` or a citext column), and compare with `where('lower(email) = ?', email.to_s.downcase)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive blocked-email lookup bug: changing an email's capitalization allows a blocked user to bypass the block. The candidate's additional indexing and normalization details do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
rejectedEmails.contains compares strictly, so the user can bypass with a case change

In `emailValidation`, `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` is a strict equality check. The list is populated from `result.values.email`, which is whatever the server stored (case preserved). If the server previously rejected `Bad@Spam.com`, the user simply retypes `bad@spam.com` and the client-side check passes, even though the backend has the same case-sensitivity bug as `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. Lowercase both the stored and compared values (e.g., store `result.values.email.toLowerCase()` and compare `email.toLowerCase()` against the list) so client-side rejection matches the address the user is currently typing.

EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch; whitelist and blacklist are untested

EmailValidator#validate_each has three independent branches (whitelist, blacklist, BlockedEmail) but the spec only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts on the blocked-email path. There is no test that an email matching `email_domains_whitelist` passes, an email outside the whitelist fails with `user.email.not_allowed`, an email matching `email_domains_blacklist` fails, that the two settings do not interact unexpectedly when both are set, or that a nil/blank value is tolerated. Regressions in any of those branches — including the `elsif` ordering that means a non-empty whitelist silently disables the blacklist — will go undetected.

Spec asserts a single increment that production does not produce

The shared example `when a BlockedEmail record matches` calls `subject` once (which calls `should_block?` once) and asserts `match_count` changes by exactly 1. In production `should_block?` is invoked from `User#valid?` and again from `User#save`, so the same signup attempt actually increments by 2. The test passes because it bypasses the validator and exercises the model method directly, masking the doubled-write bug. Add a test that mirrors the controller path (build a User with a blocked email, call `valid?` then `save`, and assert the resulting `match_count`) so the inflated-count issue is caught at the spec level.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property -ms-align-items in align-items mixin

The generated rule `-ms-align-items: $alignment;` is not a valid CSS property. The correct IE10 flexbox prefix is `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted on the line above. `-ms-align-items` will be silently ignored by IE10 and IE11, providing no cross-browser benefit while bloating the compiled CSS. This is almost certainly a typo of `-ms-flex-align`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify -ms-align-items as an invalid property and -ms-flex-align as the correct legacy replacement, so they describe the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid CSS property -webkit-align-items in align-items mixin

The generated rule `-webkit-align-items: $alignment;` is not a valid CSS property and will be silently ignored by browsers. WebKit/Blink supports the unprefixed `align-items` property directly since Chrome 21 (no transitional `-webkit-align-items` was ever shipped). The 2009 flexbox variant `-webkit-box-align` is already included on the preceding line, so this line is redundant noise that bloats the output and signals the author misunderstood the prefix matrix.

Invalid CSS property -webkit-order in order mixin

The generated rule `-webkit-order: $val;` is not a valid CSS property. WebKit/Blink has supported the unprefixed `order` property since the 2012 flexbox spec shipped in Chrome 21; no `-webkit-order` transitional prefix was ever used in production browsers. The 2009-spec prefix `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` is already emitted above. This line is dead weight that ignores the actual prefix set and suggests the author did not verify the prefixed property names.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper has no effect — parent is not a flex container

`@include order(2)` is applied to `.extra-info-wrapper`, but its parent `#topic-title` (defined earlier in the same file) is not a flex container: `.title-wrapper` still uses `float: left; width: 90%;` and there is no `display: flex` (or `@include flexbox()`) on `#topic-title` or any of its ancestors in this stylesheet. The CSS `order` property only takes effect on flex items, so this call is effectively dead code and the intended reordering will not happen. Either the parent selector must be promoted to a flex container (and `.title-wrapper`'s float/width reverted) or the `order(2)` call should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing question mark — dead code

The new `include_website_name` method is defined without the trailing `?`. Throughout this file (and AMS conventions used by Discourse), every include predicate is named `include_<attr>?` (e.g., `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_stats?`). Without the `?` the serializer never calls this method, so it has no effect and `website_name` will be included in the JSON whenever its computed value is non-nil. It should be `def include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It omits the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
TL0 users' website_name leaks to anonymous viewers

`:website` is registered with `untrusted_attributes`, which auto-generates `include_website?` to return `false` when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` (i.e., a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous/staff-with-restriction visitor). The new `include_website_name?` predicate (or the existing `include_website_name` if it's a typo) only checks `website.present?` and never calls `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. As a result, even when `website` is suppressed from the payload for a TL0 user, `website_name` (which still reveals the host and path the user has set) can still be serialized, bypassing the same privacy gate. Either add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` call (lines 105–111) or have the include predicate return `false if scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

website_name drops query string and fragment

`website_name` concatenates `URI(website).host` with `URI(website).path`, but never appends `.query` or `.fragment`. A user whose website is, e.g., `http://example.com/users/bob?tab=posts#about` will be displayed as `example.com/users/bob`, losing information the PR title advertises ('show complete URL path'). If the intent really is to mirror the original full URL when on the same domain, `URI(website).request_uri` (or host + path + query + fragment) should be used instead of just path.

No coverage that website_name is hidden from anonymous viewers of TL0 users

The 'with a TL0 user seen as anonymous' context asserts that `untrusted_attributes` (`:bio_raw`, `:bio_cooked`, `:bio_excerpt`, `:location`, `:website`, `:profile_background`, `:card_background`) are absent from `json`. After this change `:website_name` carries the same private information as `:website` and must be excluded by the same `restrict_user_fields?` gate, but the existing assertion was not extended and no new test exercises this case. Without such a test the privacy regression described above can be reintroduced unnoticed.

URI(website.to_s) parsed up to three times per call

`URI(website.to_s)` is invoked three times inside `website_name` (once for `.host`, then again for `.path` in each branch that includes the path). Each call constructs and parses a URI object. The value should be assigned to a local once (e.g., `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil`) and reused. The method is called for every user serialization, so this multiplies unnecessarily.

Drive-by doc comment change unrelated to PR

This PR is about changing the website display behaviour. The diff also edits the JSDoc above `profileBackground` from `@property websiteName` to `@property profileBackground` in `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/user.js.es6`. The fix is correct, but it's an unrelated drive-by change that should be in its own commit/PR so the website-domain UX change stays focused and reviewable.

Subdomain check uses brittle two-segment suffix test

The `elsif` branch only fires when `discourse_host` and `website_host` have the same number of dot-separated segments and that count is `> 2`. A case such as `Discourse.current_hostname` returning `example.com` (2 segments) while `website_host` is `forums.example.com` (3 segments) skips the `elsif`, drops into `else`, and `discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)` is false, so the user sees just `forums.example.com` with no path even though the discourse host is a parent suffix of the website host. The condition that decides whether to show the path should be based purely on suffix relationship (e.g., one host ends with `.` + the other, or they are equal), not on equal segment counts, otherwise same-domain path display is missed in mixed-depth subdomain setups.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match, allowing spoofed origins

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any event whose origin contains `discourseUrl` as a substring. Anything like `https://attacker.com/?x=https://discourse.host`, or any subdomain/hostname that embeds the literal, passes the check, and the parent's height (or anything else e.data ever carries) can be set by an attacker frame. Because this same message handler also reads any e.data.type, a malicious frame could trigger other branches later. Use `new URL(discourseUrl).origin` (with a trailing slash check) and compare exactly: `new URL(e.origin).origin === expectedOrigin`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify insecure substring-based postMessage origin validation using indexOf, allowing untrusted origins to pass instead of requiring exact origin equality. The candidate misstates the substring direction and gives questionable examples, but identifies the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Stored XSS: untrusted RSS content stored with raw_html cook_method

poll_feed reads `i.content` from the feed, runs only `CGI.unescapeHTML(...scrub)` (which strips invalid bytes but does not sanitize HTML), and passes it straight into `TopicEmbed.import`. import then creates a post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and, because Post#cook returns `raw` for that mode and best.html.erb renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, any `<script>` (or other active) tags in the feed end up executing inside an iframe whose origin is Discourse. The same vector exists for TopicEmbed.import_remote (Readability output is trusted and the raw URL body for Disqus) and the disqus.thor import. Anyone with admin control of feed_polling_url (or embeddable_host, or a Disqus import file) can get script execution in Discourse's origin and read cookies / take actions on behalf of logged-in users visiting the embed iframe. The fix is to never assign raw_html to imported posts from external sources; run them through the normal cook/sanitize pipeline.

New cook_method column default of 1 likely marks every existing post as raw_html

The migration adds `cook_method integer default 1 not null` to posts. Post.cook_methods is `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` and Post#cook short-circuits to `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. With conventional (0-indexed) Enum implementations `[:regular] == 0` and `[:raw_html] == 1`, so existing rows default to raw_html, which means Post#cook now returns the unprocessed markdown source. The before_save hook does `self.cooked = cook(raw, topic_id: topic_id) unless new_record?`, so the next edit on any existing post will overwrite `cooked` with raw markdown and visibly break rendering across the entire site. The migration default should be whichever value Enum maps to `:regular` (verify the Enum implementation; it is almost certainly 0, not 1).

embed/best does not validate that embed_url belongs to the embeddable host

`embed_url = params.require(:embed_url)` is used directly in `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and passed to `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, embed_url: embed_url)` without verifying its host equals `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The host check happens only asynchronously inside TopicRetriever. Anyone who knows an existing embed_url can render that topic via `/embed/best`, and any caller can enqueue a retrieve for a non-matching URL (it just silently no-ops in the retriever, but still hits the DB, the queue, and reveals embed existence). Validate the host synchronously in the controller before doing the lookup or enqueueing.

Imported posts created with skip_validations: true and raw_html can persist arbitrary content with no Sanitize pass

When `TopicEmbed.import` creates the initial post it passes `skip_validations: true` along with `cook_method: raw_html`. Combined, the post's `cooked` field stores whatever HTML the caller supplied, including `<script>`, `onerror=`, `<iframe>`, javascript: links, etc., and Post#cook then returns that raw content unmolested. Even though `absolutize_urls` runs on the content, it does not sanitize. Two follow-up problems: (1) the Disqus thor path later creates further reply posts via PostCreator without setting `cook_method`, mixing modes in the same topic; (2) `revisor.revise!(... , skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` overwrites the post with whatever the next import produces, also bypassed. Sanitize imported HTML before storing it and do not pair `skip_validations` with raw_html.

Synchronously executes the scheduled PollFeed job on every retrieve

`perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inside the retriever job's execution. This pulls and parses the full RSS feed, hits RSS hosts, and writes TopicEmbeds for every item in the feed, all while the retriever itself (triggered by a user GET to /embed/best) is queued behind it. A large feed will make every embed request stall, and it ignores the PollFeed scheduling/throttling guarantees. The retrieve should only try to import the single embed_url, not rerun the whole feed poller inline.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Two `def self.downsize` definitions silently shadow each other

Lines 145 and 149 both define `def self.downsize(...)`. Ruby does not support method overloading; the second definition (line 149) replaces the first (line 145). Any existing caller that previously invoked `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` will now dispatch to the new method, with the integer `max_width` being interpreted as a pre-formatted dimensions string and `max_height` being put inside the opts hash. This silently breaks every existing caller of the 4-argument form, and the now-redundant definition on line 145 should be removed (or renamed) before merging.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the later dimensions-string version overrides the earlier width-and-height version, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers. The candidate's additional argument-handling claims do not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
