Client-side upload size check is hardcoded to 10MB and ignores site settings

validateUploadedFile now uses `var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024;` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. If a site admin configures a different limit, users will be blocked from uploading files the server would accept, or allowed to upload files the server rejects.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10MB limit replacing per-type site settings and the resulting mismatch between client and server upload limits. Omitting the additional 413-handler reference does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

Animated-GIF downsize path passes an invalid dimensions value to gifsicle

When SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is true, OptimizedImage.optimize routes through downsize_instructions_animated, which builds `gifsicle ... --resize-fit #{dimensions} ...`. The controller passes the literal string `"80%"` as dimensions, but gifsicle's `--resize-fit` flag expects pixel dimensions of the form `WxH`, not a percentage. The animated-GIF auto-downsize path will fail or resize to nonsensical dimensions, defeating the feature for the very case the SiteSetting is meant to support.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit in the animated GIF path when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, even though that flag requires WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedImage.downsize is called with the same path for input and output

The auto-downsize loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...). The underlying convert (or gifsicle, for animated GIFs) command then opens the file for reading and writing at the same path. ImageMagick and gifsicle will truncate the destination before reading from it, which can produce an empty or corrupt output file. The next call to Upload.create_for will then persist a zero-byte or garbled image with no error surfaced to the caller or user.

The case-413 branch now shows the user `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` irrespective of the actual server-side cap. When the server's effective limit differs from 10MB (because max_image_size_kb or the new download cap has been reconfigured), the error dialog misreports the threshold the user must satisfy. The user-facing message is now decoupled from the server's real limit.

URL download size cap is hardcoded to 10MB instead of using the site setting

FileHelper.download is now called with `10.megabytes` instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. The download cap is no longer configurable via the same knob as the rest of the upload flow, and any site whose configured `max_image_size_kb` differs from 10MB will see inconsistent behaviour between direct uploads and URL-sourced fetches. Given the new auto-downsize feature is supposed to let images larger than `max_image_size_kb` through, the download cap should be raised above that setting (or made explicit), not silently frozen at 10MB.

The while loop re-checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` but never inspects the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. OptimizedImage.convert_with rescues every error and returns false on failure (e.g., ImageMagick not installed, corrupt source), but the controller discards that signal and only decrements `attempt`. If all five iterations fail, the upload proceeds with a file that may still exceed the configured limit — or be empty/corrupt from the failed in-place rewrite — and the user receives no indication that auto-resize failed.

The new block is gated on `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`. For URL-sourced uploads the filename is derived from `File.basename(URI.parse(url).path)`, which frequently does not reflect the actual response (e.g., a JPEG served as `download.bin` or `attachment`). Real images with non-image filenames will skip auto-downsize and may exceed the configured limit, while non-image files masquerading as `.jpg` will be piped through OptimizedImage.downsize and likely corrupted by ImageMagick before being persisted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
GET request mutates user state, bypassing CSRF protection

The new `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) but it mutates state (changes `TopicUser#notification_level` and calls `save!`). Rails only checks CSRF tokens for non-GET requests, so any third-party page, image, link prefetch, or email preview that causes a logged-in user to issue a GET to these URLs will silently change that user's notification level. By contrast the existing `set_notifications` endpoint in this same controller correctly uses `post`. This new action must be POST/DELETE (or use a signed one-time token) and use Rails' `protect_from_forgery`/`verify_authenticity_token` flow.

`ensure_logged_in` makes the email unsubscribe link unusable

The whole point of this feature is the link the user receives in a notification email. The new `:unsubscribe` action is added to the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` list and the route is a plain GET, so any recipient who clicks the unsubscribe link from their mail client without an active Discourse session is bounced to the login page instead of being unsubscribed. Standard email one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058) requires an authenticated-by-token flow; here the URL must carry a per-user, per-topic signed secret that authorises the notification change without requiring a login.

Toggle logic downgrades watching/tracking only to `regular`, so the user keeps getting emails

The branch `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` sets the level to `:regular` (which still sends notifications) for users who were `:watching` or `:tracking`. The only path that actually stops emails is the `else` branch (regular/muted -> muted). Users who were actively watching the topic and click 'unsubscribe' will continue receiving notification emails, which is the opposite of what the link promises. The action should mute (or apply the level chosen by the user via the page UI) rather than treat the operation as a `>= regular ? regular : muted` toggle.

Bypassing `TopicUser.change` skips the `MessageBus` publish and reason tracking

`TopicUser.change` is the existing canonical way to mutate a `TopicUser` row: it sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` when `notification_level` changes, publishes `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` so other tabs/clients update in real time, and creates the row when missing. This controller fetches the row, mutates the attribute, and calls `save!`, so (a) no `MessageBus` event is fired (open clients keep showing the old level), (b) `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not refreshed, and (c) any race where the row is deleted between `find_by` and `save!` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. The action should delegate to `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`.

Action renders the topic page instead of acknowledging the unsubscribe

After mutating the notification level, the action falls through to `perform_show_response`, which renders the normal topic view. The user (who came from an email expecting a confirmation) is dropped on the regular topic page with no visible feedback that anything happened, and the URL they bookmark/share contains `/unsubscribe`. There is no redirect to a confirmation screen and no flash/notice. Either render a dedicated confirmation view or redirect to a stable page that reflects the new state.

No tests cover the new per-topic unsubscribe URL in the email body

The new `unsubscribe_link` server locale adds a `%{unsubscribe_url}` markdown link (`To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})`), and `user_notifications.rb` now passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. The updated spec only asserts that the existing `user_preferences_url` is present; there is no expectation that the new `unsubscribe_url` is actually rendered into the body, nor any test for `Topic#unsubscribe_url`, `TopicsController#unsubscribe`, or the `notification_level` change behaviour. Add a test that the body contains the topic unsubscribe URL and that `Topic#unsubscribe_url` returns the expected path.

`bottom: initial` is unlikely to do what was intended

The new rule `.topic-unsubscribe .notification-options .dropdown-menu { bottom: initial; }` uses the CSS-wide keyword `initial`, resetting `bottom` to its initial value (i.e. `auto`). That just undoes any prior offset and is almost certainly not the intent — the goal was presumably to override the default dropdown placement for the embedded button on the unsubscribe page. Use an explicit value (`auto`, `100%`, or a measured offset) instead of `initial`, otherwise the rule is effectively a no-op.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
macOS-only sed syntax breaks script on Linux

Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E "..."` which is BSD/macOS sed syntax. On Linux, `sed -i` requires either no argument or a suffix as an extension (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E`). As written, the script will fail with a usage error on any non-macOS developer machine or CI runner, silently leaving `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` stale and breaking local webhook testing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: BSD/macOS-style `sed -i ''` fails on Linux systems.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste bug in working-hours end calculation

In the newly added working-hours check inside `checkIfIsAvailable`, `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. As `start === end`, the guard collapses to `slotStartTime < workingHour.startTime || slotStartTime > workingHour.endTime`, which never detects slots whose duration crosses the end of the working window. For any event longer than the gap between the slot start and the day's working-hour end (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting at 17:30 with working hours 9-17), the slot is treated as inside working hours and forwarded to the busy check, so it can be booked outside availability.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the end time is calculated using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, matching the golden comment's underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`===` on dayjs instances never matches, breaking zero-length override handling

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` is reference equality of two distinct dayjs objects, which is always false. The branch that returns `true` (treating the slot as outside the override because the override has no duration) is therefore unreachable. Use `.isSame()` or compare `.valueOf()` if the intent is a value comparison. As written, a zero-length override (or "all-day" override with equal start and end) cannot be matched and falls into the same path as ordinary ranges.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: === compares distinct dayjs object references rather than date values, making the comparison always false. Both recommend .isSame() for value comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours comparison uses UTC time/day against organizer-local working hours

The working-hours guard compares `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())`, `slotStartTime.hour()` and `slotStartTime.minute()` against `workingHour.startTime/endTime`. `WorkingHours.startTime/endTime` are minutes since midnight and `days` is the organizer/day-local day-of-week (as produced by `getAggregateWorkingHours`/`getWorkingHours`), while `slotStartTime` was produced by `time.utc()`, so `.day()/.hour()/.minute()` are in UTC. The comparison only works when organizer TZ is UTC; for any other organizer timezone the day-of-week and time-of-day values do not line up and slots can be classified as in/out of hours purely based on the UTC clock. The slot must be converted to the organizer's timezone (or, in `checkIfIsAvailable`, to `organizerTimeZone`) before these comparisons.

Date-override day comparison formats in the server's local timezone

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats the shifted instant using the dayjs instance's default (server-local) timezone, not `organizerTimeZone`. The right-hand side `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is also in the server's local zone, so the two sides happen to match each other but not necessarily the organizer. When an organizer whose timezone is east of UTC enters an early-morning override (e.g. 06:30 IST = 01:00 UTC), `add(-330)` crosses midnight and the formatted day is the previous UTC day, so slots on the correct organizer day are rejected as outside the override. Use `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")` and `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")` to compare days in the organizer's timezone.

Multi-override semantics: first non-covering override incorrectly blocks the slot

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` loop returns the first override whose day matches and for which the slot is outside that override's range; the outer `if` then returns `false` (slot unavailable) regardless of whether another override for the same day does cover the slot. With several date overrides on the same day (e.g. 09-11 and 14-16), a slot at 09:30 is inside the first override but not the second, the find returns the second, and the slot is rejected. The semantic should be ANY (available if any override covers), not ALL. The simplest fix is to break out as soon as a covering override is found, and only return `false` if every override for that day fails to cover.

`dayjs.tz(date.start, override.timeZone)` used without guarding undefined

`override.timeZone` was just made optional on `TimeRange`, but `slots.ts` calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` unconditionally. `dayjs.tz(..., undefined)` does not throw on every code path but yields the host-local offset, which silently corrupts the offset math (`organizerUtcOffset`) and therefore every converted override time, producing wrong `startTime`/`endTime` minutes and wrong slots. Either require `timeZone` on the input, default it to `organizerTimeZone`/`timeZone`, or assert/throw when it is missing so the failure is not silent.

Convoluted offset arithmetic obscures intent and is easy to break under DST

`const utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1;` followed by `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` is a non-standard way to express "view `date.start` in `organizerTimeZone`". It also relies on the offset at the exact instant `date.start`, so for multi-day date overrides that span a DST transition the start and end can be shifted by different amounts and the resulting window can be subtly incorrect. Replacing this with `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone)` (and equivalent on the slot) eliminates the manual offset handling.

No test for the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR description and linked issues (#8207, #8329) state the change makes fixed hosts' date overrides count toward round-robin availability, but the new test only covers a single user with a date override at two different invitee timezones. There is no scenario that exercises a round-robin event with a fixed host plus a round-robin host where the fixed host has a date override restricting availability on a day; that is precisely the behaviour being fixed and currently has no regression test.

New `workingHours` branch in `checkIfIsAvailable` has no coverage

The PR adds a `workingHours`-based availability check inside `checkIfIsAvailable` (slots.ts lines 138-151). None of the tests in `getSchedule.test.ts` cover that branch (no test sets up a schedule with a normal-hours entry and then exercises a slot that crosses or falls outside those hours, and none cover the UTC-vs-organizer-tz interaction). Given the day/time-of-day handling bugs above, this is the branch most likely to regress silently and is exactly where a regression test belongs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increment is read-modify-write and not atomic

The update uses `data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 }`, where `reminder.retryCount` was read earlier in `findMany`. If two cron invocations (or any concurrent process) process the same reminder, both will read the same value and both will write `value + 1`, silently losing one retry attempt and possibly keeping a failing reminder alive beyond the intended two attempts. Use Prisma's atomic `increment` operation (e.g. `update({ where: { id }, data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } } })`) in both the `else` branch (line 179-186) and the `catch` branch (line 190-197).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same stale read-modify-write race that can lose retryCount increments under concurrency and recommends Prisma's atomic increment in both the main update and catch block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup deleteMany applies retryCount > 1 to non-SMS reminders too

The new cleanup `deleteMany` uses an `OR` whose second branch is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. The first branch is correctly scoped to SMS, but the second branch will delete any `WorkflowReminder` row (including EMAIL and WHATSAPP) whose `retryCount` exceeds 1, regardless of scheduledDate. Today only this SMS path increments `retryCount`, but any future change that bumps the counter for email/whatsapp (or a stray backfill) will silently delete those reminders too. The retryCount clause should be `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 }` to keep semantics consistent with the rest of the handler.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 branch of the deletion OR clause, which can delete non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:
retryCount never incremented when message or sendTo is empty, so the new retry/delete mechanism is bypassed

The new retry/delete behavior only fires inside the branches that actually attempt scheduling. When `message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo` is falsy (e.g. SMS template evaluates to an empty string, attendee has no phone number, etc.) the entire `if` block is skipped, no `twilio.scheduleSMS` call is made, and neither the `else` (line 179) nor the `catch` (line 190) path runs. The reminder therefore never has its `retryCount` incremented and will be picked up again on every cron run until its `scheduledDate` passes, exactly the bug this PR claims to fix. The PR description's stated goal is to delete reminders that fail to schedule after two attempts, so empty message / missing recipient must also drive `retryCount` (e.g. increment in an `else` for the outer guard) or be deleted immediately.

SMS scheduling errors are logged with console.log instead of console.error

The catch block at line 198 uses `console.log(`Error scheduling SMS with error ${error}`)`. Failure logs should use `console.error` so they are routed to error streams/aggregators and don't get buried in routine info output; otherwise on-call engineers triaging SMS delivery issues have to grep for the string "Error scheduling" in info-level logs.

No tests added for the new retryCount / cleanup behavior

The PR introduces a new `retryCount` column, a new cleanup branch in `deleteMany` (`retryCount > 1`), and new increment paths in both the `else` and `catch` branches. None of these are covered by automated tests. Given there are several failure paths (twilio returns falsy, twilio throws, message empty, sendTo missing) and a non-trivial boundary (`gt: 1` rather than `gte: 1`), this is a regression risk. Tests should at minimum cover: SMS scheduled successfully -> `scheduled: true` set; twilio returns falsy -> `retryCount` becomes 1, reminder still present; twilio throws -> `retryCount` becomes 1; reminder with `retryCount >= 2` is deleted by the cleanup `deleteMany`; the empty message / missing sendTo case actually increments `retryCount` (or is fixed to do so per the other finding).

findMany method removed without migration path

The previously-public `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method has been deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions()`. Any existing caller (other modules, route handlers, etc.) that previously invoked `service.findMany({ select, where, orderBy, take, ... })` will now fail to compile, and the README/PR description does not document this as a breaking change nor provide a migration shim. A search for other consumers should be done before merging and any callers must be updated to use `prisma.$queryRaw` with the returned conditions.

Loss of where-clause merging capability

The previous `findMany` merged a caller's `findManyArgs.where` into the final Prisma where (via `...findManyArgs.where, AND: [auth, filter]`). The new `getBaseConditions()` only returns the authorization + filter SQL fragment and provides no way for a caller to layer additional predicates. Any caller that relied on passing extra `where` (date ranges, status filters, paging cursor, etc.) will silently lose those filters. The integration test now hard-codes a `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized"` query and the call sites have no documented API to add their own conditions.

Caching behaviour no longer covered by tests

The previous test file contained a `describe("Caching", ...)` block with two tests that verified `getAuthorizationConditions` / `getFilterConditions` returned identical objects on repeated calls (proving the internal cache works). The new diff silently removes that entire describe block while the cache (`this.cachedAuthConditions`, `this.cachedFilterConditions`) is still implemented in the service. There is no replacement test, so regressions to the cache (e.g. accidental double work, or cache not invalidating after construction) would not be caught. The PR description does not mention removing this coverage.

Integration test depends on BookingTimeStatusDenormalized being synchronously populated

The integration test inserts rows via `prisma.booking.create` / `prisma.eventType.create` and immediately runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}`, expecting the just-inserted booking to appear. This relies on `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` being kept in sync with `Booking` synchronously (via trigger or denormalization job at insert time). If it is a materialized view or is only refreshed by a background job, this test will be flaky in CI. The PR description even acknowledges that the test runner had configuration issues and asks for manual verification. There is no setup/teardown that guarantees the denormalized table reflects the freshly created booking, and no assertion that the table is non-empty before running the test.

Prisma.Sql equality assertions are fragile and not validated

Every assertion in the rewritten test compares the service output with a literal `Prisma.sql\`...\`` template using `expect(...).toEqual(...)`. `Prisma.Sql` is an object whose internal `strings` / `values` arrays are sensitive to whitespace, parenthesis placement, and the order of interpolation. Several assertions in the diff (e.g. line 273, 296-298, 333-343) embed `${[array]}` exactly matching the implementation's array order; if the implementation ever produces a different equivalent SQL (e.g. `("teamId" = ANY($1))` vs `("teamId" = $1)` for a single element, or different spacing) the tests will fail even though the SQL is semantically identical. There is no helper that compares the rendered SQL structurally, and the PR description explicitly flags that the tests were not actually run (`test runner configuration issues`) so the equality assumptions are unverified.

Constructor type widened without enforcing teamId for team scope

The constructor parameter type changed from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (discriminated union that requires `teamId` when `scope === "team"`) to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` where `teamId` is optional. `safeParse` then sets `this.options = null` on any validation failure, which silently downgrades the user to `NOTHING_CONDITION` (no results) instead of throwing. A caller that passes `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without `teamId` will get a service that returns nothing with no error. This is a behaviour change: previously TypeScript would reject the call at compile time; now it silently produces empty results, which is a security/visibility concern since it may mask authorization bugs.

PR description mislabels the scope of the change

The PR title and description say this only "updates the integration tests for the Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation", but the diff also substantially rewrites the service itself: deletes `findMany`, changes return types from `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` to `Prisma.Sql`, widens the constructor options type, removes the `NOTHING = { id: -1 }` sentinel, and adds `getBaseConditions()`. Reviewers reading the description would not expect these breaking service-level changes. The description should be updated to call out the API break and the removal of cache tests.

- `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177,192`: does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(...)`. A fetch `Response` has no `expiryDate`; this throws and the token is never saved.
- `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`: does `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. A `Response` has no `.data`, so this throws and the credential update is skipped.

Either the helper should `await refreshFunction()` (i.e. only short-circuit when syncing) or every caller must be updated to consume a `Response`.

`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so a network attacker measuring response latency can recover the secret byte by byte. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) since the secret is high-value.

Wrap the lookup-and-write in a Prisma transaction (or upsert with a unique key) and consider de-duplicating webhooks.

The sync endpoint should authenticate Cal.com with a shared secret header, and the response should be authenticated/signed too. Also, `calcomUserId` is sent in the URL body - consider sending it in a signed payload.

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` has no `signal`/timeout, so if the sync endpoint is unresponsive Cal.com's token refresh path blocks indefinitely, which in turn blocks every booking/Calendar availability check for that user. `const workflowRemindersToDelete: Prisma.Prisma__WorkflowReminderClient<WorkflowReminder, never>[] = [];` references a private/internal Prisma generated type (`Prisma__WorkflowReminderClient`). `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); }))` does not await the async reminder calls. The handler returns the success response while cancellations are still in flight. Errors from the internal `try/catch` of those helpers are merely logged via `console.log` and the caller never learns if a cancellation failed. Combined with the immediateDelete semantics, a failure means the cancelled booking can still trigger an outgoing workflow reminder. Convert to `await Promise.all(...)` or sequential `for/await`.

Reschedule reminder cancellation not awaited

In `requestReschedule`, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); })` does not await the async deletion calls. Failures are only logged by the helpers' internal catch and never propagated to the caller, so a SendGrid/Prisma error leaves the reminder in place. Several blocks in the `update` and `delete` mutations (`scheduledReminders.forEach`, `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach`, `remindersFromStep.forEach`, `remindersToUpdate.forEach`, `steps.forEach` calling `scheduleEmailReminder`/`scheduleSMSReminder`) iterate with `forEach` over async functions that are never awaited. Errors from SendGrid/Twilio/Prisma are swallowed inside the helpers' catch blocks. Cancellation loop is sequential

Reminders are cancelled one at a time using `await client.request(...)` inside a `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop. With many reminders to cancel (the whole reason for deferring to a CRON), serializing SendGrid calls slows the CRON. The SendGrid cancel calls are independent, so they can run in parallel via `Promise.allSettled` to keep the request window short and reduce the chance that one slow call blocks the run. The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to `1` and its help string says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' It will therefore map, for instance, `messages_zh_TW.properties` to `messages_en.properties` instead of `messages_zh_Hant.properties`/etc., and will silently turn `messages_.properties` into `messages_en.properties`. When the English source happens to use uppercase tags, POLICY_NO_HTML is incorrectly selected and the OWASP sanitizer is then forced to make a structural decision that POLICY_SOME_HTML was meant to handle, producing false positives. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Finer-grain cache lock lets two callers build the same index concurrently

After this PR, bleveBackend.BuildIndex only takes cacheMu around the final map assignment (`b.cache[key] = idx`); the actual index creation (bleve.New/bleve.NewMemOnly and the ListIterator walk) runs unlocked. getOrCreateIndex itself has no synchronization, so two concurrent callers with the same NamespacedResource can both observe an empty cache (GetIndex returns nil), both call s.build, each constructs its own bleveIndex (running through the storage ListIterator independently), and then both contend on b.cacheMu — last writer wins. Each caller uses its own freshly built index for its Search/Origin call, so the cache may not reflect what the first caller is actually using, and the second caller's build duplicates work that was just done; if storage changes between the two walks the two indexes can diverge. Add per-key locking (e.g., a sync.Map of *sync.Mutex keyed by NamespacedResource, or use sync.Map directly) so only one goroutine builds a given index and other callers wait for it to be cached.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: cacheMu was narrowed to protect only the final assignment, so concurrent callers can build the same index for the same key in duplicate.

false_positives.candidate:
search.init goroutine panics when the events channel is closed

In the goroutine started by search.init, the receive `v := <-events` is not in the comma-ok form, and the loop then unconditionally calls `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)`. The SQL backend closes the events channel via `defer close(stream)` when its poller returns (e.g., when backend.Stop calls cancel and `b.done` closes). After that, every iteration of the for loop receives nil for `v` (zero value of *WrittenEvent), and `s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil)` then dereferences `evt.Type` on a nil receiver, panicking the goroutine. Because the search watch is now started eagerly inside NewResourceServer on every startup, the lifecycle that closes this channel is reached on every shutdown. The receive should be `v, ok := <-events` with `if !ok { return }` so the goroutine terminates cleanly when the backend is torn down.

search.init watch goroutine is not bound to the server's lifecycle

search.init sets `watchctx := context.Background()` and passes it to `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)`, then spawns a goroutine that processes events with this background context. This context is completely independent of the server's cancellable context (`s.ctx`, which server.Stop cancels via s.cancel). Calling server.Stop therefore does not stop the search watch goroutine; it only terminates once the SQL backend itself is torn down (b.cancel) and the poller's defer closes the events channel. Combined with the missing comma-ok on the channel receive (related finding above), the goroutine can panic during shutdown rather than exit cleanly. The watch should be tied to a context derived from s.ctx so server.Stop halts search indexing promptly, and the backend poller should respect that context for cancellation.

Two independent database pollers run for WatchWriteEvents

Both search.init (search.go ~line 203) and server.initWatcher call s.backend.WatchWriteEvents, and the SQL backend starts a separate poller goroutine for each call. Each poller runs `listLatestRVs` plus per-resource `poll` queries against the database every defaultPollingInterval (100ms), producing essentially the same event stream. With both watchers active the backend is doing two full sets of polls for what could be a single shared source. Before this PR these two watchers were also started, but lazily on the first gRPC call; after this PR they are both started eagerly and synchronously inside NewResourceServer, so this 2x DB load is now paid on every startup. Consider having a single backend.WatchWriteEvents source that fans out to the search index and the broadcaster (e.g., a shared channel that searchSupport.handleEvent and the broadcaster both subscribe to).

Postgres branch is skipped instead of fixed in the integration test

The new lines `// TODO - fix this test for postgres` plus `t.Skip(...)` for GRAFANA_TEST_DB == "postgres" hide a real test reliability problem rather than fixing it. Now that NewResourceServer blocks on Init during module server construction, this code path is more sensitive to slow or failing init, which is plausibly contributing to the CI failure (the comment says "Works locally" but not in Drone). A skip only papers over the failure: the postgres path is no longer exercised at all in CI, so future regressions on it will go unnoticed. The TODO should be tracked and the test should actually run for postgres in CI, or the broader problem should be diagnosed (e.g., separate slow init in NewResourceServer from module server startup so the test has a chance to complete).

Every `AssignmentSource` constructed without an explicit `queued` argument will share the same timestamp (the time the module was first imported). It should be `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` imported from `dataclasses`). The field is currently unused in the sync logic so the impact is low, but it is incorrect and will surprise anyone who later relies on `queued` for ordering, TTL, or debugging.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. The AssignmentSource dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition, so every instance shares the same timestamp.

false_positives.candidate:
`from_dict` silently swallows all errors and returns None

`AssignmentSource.from_dict` uses a bare `except (ValueError, TypeError)` and returns `None` for any malformed payload. This is unsafe because the only signal callers get is `None`, which is treated identically to "no assignment source was provided", meaning `should_sync` will happily allow the outbound sync to proceed. Concrete risks: (a) forward-compatibility — if a new required field is added to `AssignmentSource` later, every in-flight Celery task whose `assignment_source_dict` predates the change will silently deserialize to `None`, re-enabling the very sync cycle this PR is trying to fix; (b) corruption of task payloads will be invisible. The method should at minimum log the malformed payload, or raise so the caller can decide (e.g., retry vs. drop) instead of silently dropping the cycle-prevention signal.

`sync_status_outbound` abstract signature adds `assignment_source` that is never passed anywhere

The abstract method `sync_status_outbound` is updated to take `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller in this PR (or visible in the diff) ever passes it. The `sync_assignee_outbound` task only invokes `sync_assignee_outbound`, not `sync_status_outbound`. This is misleading: the PR description claims to break "issue sync cycles" (plural) and the new signature implies status sync cycles are being addressed, but the status cycle is not actually broken — inbound `sync_status_inbound` still triggers `sync_status_outbound` without any source guard. Any concrete implementation that does not already accept `**kwargs` will also break if a future caller does pass `assignment_source`. Either remove the parameter from the abstract signature until the status-side fix is implemented, or implement and thread the assignment_source through the status path so the cycle is actually closed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong behavior

The test sets `mock_processor_call.side_effect = [Exception('Processing failed'), None]` and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But OrderedQueueWorker.run catches the exception in the inner `except Exception` and still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in the `finally`, so offset 100 is marked completed. Offset 101 also completes. Both are contiguous, so the commit loop will commit offset 102 (101+1). The assertion as written would fail in the correct behavior, and the assertion is trivially true when `len == 0` regardless of what happened. The test should instead assert the committed offset reflects both completed messages (e.g., `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`) to actually verify the 'errors don't block other commits' intent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to an inconsistency between the test's stated intent (docstring: errors don't block commits) and its assertion in test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling. Same underlying issue, framed differently.

false_positives.candidate:
Unbounded queue with no backpressure can exhaust memory

In FixedQueuePool.__init__, the queues are created as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, making them unbounded. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (line 293) calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If a particular group is slow (e.g., a subscription whose handler hangs), all items for that group accumulate in its dedicated queue without limit. Unlike the existing `BatchStep`/`RunTask` strategies, this new strategy provides no backpressure: the main thread keeps fetching from Kafka and calling submit, so memory can grow without bound until the consumer OOMs. The PR description acknowledges that 'there's still a chance of individual items backlogging a queue' but does not bound the queue or block submit when queues are full.

get_committable_offsets iterates O(max_offset) not O(outstanding)

In OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets, the loop `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` iterates over every offset in the numeric range, even those that were never added (e.g., gaps from compaction, filtered payloads, or pre-existing committed offsets). For a partition with min_offset=0 and max_offset=1_000_000 and only a few outstanding offsets, this is ~1 million iterations per call, and the commit loop calls this once per second per partition. It should iterate over the sorted `all_offsets` set (O(k log k) where k is the number of seen offsets) and break on the first outstanding/missing one.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join silently drops timeout argument

`def join(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> None: self.close()` ignores the `timeout` parameter entirely. Arroyo's ProcessingStrategy contract allows callers to pass a join timeout (e.g., during shutdown sequencing). Silently ignoring it means callers cannot bound how long join blocks, and the strategy will always wait the full internal 5.0s for the commit thread plus however long queue_pool.shutdown takes.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown 5s join can drop in-flight work

`worker.join(timeout=5.0)` only waits 5 seconds, and the worker is a daemon so it is killed on process exit. If a `result_processor` call takes longer than 5 seconds (which is exactly the kind of slow item this PR is designed to isolate), the join times out, the daemon thread is abandoned, and any work it was holding is never reported as completed/comitted. The fix is either to use a configurable/longer timeout, to join the strategy's commit thread only after all queues drain (e.g., call `wait_until_empty` first), or to set `immediate=True` on `q.shutdown()` and document the data-loss tradeoff.

test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown does not verify graceful behavior

The test submits 5 messages and then immediately calls `factory.shutdown()` without waiting for processing, asserting only `factory.queue_pool is None`. This does not verify that the 5 submitted messages are processed before shutdown, that no offsets are lost, or that the shutdown is actually graceful. Combined with the 5s join timeout in FixedQueuePool.shutdown, this test will pass even if shutdown drops all in-flight work.

Kafka integration test depends on private StreamProcessor internals

The test drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` in a loop and `processor._shutdown()` at the end. These are private arroyo methods (leading underscore) and are not part of the public API; they can change between arroyo releases without notice, which would silently break this test. It also relies on `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` and creates real Kafka topics in a `requires_kafka` test, so it is expensive and fragile. A more robust integration test would use the public `run()` method or otherwise not depend on underscore-prefixed methods.

Unreachable queue.ShutDown handler in inner try

The inner `try` block in OrderedQueueWorker.run only wraps `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(...)` and `self.result_processor(...)`. `queue.ShutDown` can only be raised by `queue.Queue.get()` or `queue.Queue.put()`, neither of which is called inside this inner try. The `except queue.ShutDown: break` on lines 142-143 is therefore dead code and can be removed (or, if a put call is later added inside the inner try, the comment should explain why).

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative int) when `enable_advanced_features` is True. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for any negative start index, so this path can never produce results. The cursor string is parsed by `Cursor.from_string` via `int(bits[1])`, which happily accepts a negative value, so any client (or a hand-crafted cursor) can trigger the crash. Combined with the `organization_auditlogs.py` change that always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, the new admin endpoint is a guaranteed `AssertionError` whenever the resulting cursor has offset < 0.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same code path: get_result in OptimizedCursorPaginator passes a negative cursor.offset straight into queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True. The candidate adds that Django raises an AssertionError on negative slices, but it is the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misleading 'Performance optimization' comment for a behavior change

The change in `BasePaginator.get_result` from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` is a small behavioral fix, not a performance optimization. The new `max(0, offset)` call is essentially free and does not reduce query cost; it just prevents an `AssertionError` for negative non-prev cursors. The inline comment 'Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets...' is misleading and should describe the actual change (clamping negative non-prev offsets to 0 to avoid a crash). Also note the asymmetry: prev cursors are NOT clamped, so a negative prev cursor will still crash in Django — the two branches should behave consistently.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main point is the misleading comment. It also says outright that prev cursors are not clamped, so a negative prev offset still reaches Django slicing and crashes. That is the same issue as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000, breaking deep segment trees

The loop bound was tightened from 10000 to 1000 while the explanatory comment about depth-10k trees was deleted. The redirect hash chain can still legitimately reach depths above 1000 (the data didn't change), so once `redirect_depth >= 1000` the loop exits early without resolving to a fixed point. The script then writes a `hset` mapping this span's id to an unresolved intermediate `set_span_id` and unions it into the wrong set, so subsequent children of the segment will land in a different buffer key. Result: spans get split across multiple `span-buf:s:*` keys instead of being joined into one segment — segments will be flushed incomplete or duplicated, directly causing data loss/duplication. The previous bound (and its comment) should be preserved unless the maximum possible redirect depth has been proven to be bounded below 1000.

Spans are silently evicted at insert time without any metric or log

After merging incoming spans into `set_key`, the script does `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`. There is no `redis.call('incrby', ...)` for a metric, no log, and the corresponding `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Spans are silently dropped from the segment with zero observability. Worse, the eviction is by lowest `end_timestamp_precise` score, which is not necessarily the spans that are safe to drop (a parent span sent late would have a later score than its children and be kept, while a root span sent early could be evicted, leaving the segment without a root and causing it to fall through to the long `span_buffer_timeout_secs` path or be flushed incomplete). The threshold 1000 also does not match `max_segment_spans=1001` configured on `SpansBuffer`. At minimum this needs a counter (e.g. `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.evicted', n)`), a log when eviction occurs, and a guarantee that the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved.

OptimizedCursorPaginator has no working behavior beyond BasePaginator

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class duplicates almost all of `BasePaginator.get_result` and the only behavior change is the negative-offset branch. Because that branch cannot work (Django rejects negative slicing, see other finding), `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is functionally identical to `BasePaginator`. The `enable_advanced_features=True` flag exposed via `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` therefore does nothing useful in production. The PR title is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'; this entire paginator/auditlog change is unrelated and should be split out. As shipped it adds dead code, a misleading admin-only API knob, and a guaranteed crash path.

Required `end_timestamp_precise` field added to Span NamedTuple is a contract break

`Span` is a public NamedTuple. Adding `end_timestamp_precise: float` before the defaulted `is_segment_span: bool = False` makes it a required positional argument and breaks every existing `Span(...)` call site that does not supply it (TypeError). All in-repo callers in this PR are updated, but there are likely other consumers (snuba-spans ingestion, tests outside this PR, downstream internal tools) that construct `Span` instances directly. Any such caller will now crash at module/import time on first use, and any older serialized payload that doesn't carry `end_timestamp_precise` will now KeyError inside `process_batch`. This change should either default to `0.0`/`None` or have a clearly documented migration; missing-field handling in `process_batch` is not implemented.

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path

Tests under `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` and `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py` only ever add ~4 spans per segment. The new Lua eviction kicks in at >1000 spans, which is now the actual hard cap on segment size (the Python `max_segment_spans` check was removed), yet nothing exercises it. A test that ingests >1000 spans into one segment is needed to assert: (a) eviction actually happens, (b) the root span (or HRS flag) is preserved, (c) a metric is emitted so the silent-drop path is observable. Without this, regressions in the eviction behavior would land silently.

ZADD uses payload bytes as member; duplicate payloads are silently dropped

Switching the segment from `sadd` to `zadd` keeps the same 'member = span.payload (bytes)' model. Sorted sets require unique members, so two spans whose serialized payloads happen to be byte-identical (e.g. retries, duplicate Kafka messages, or same span replayed) will be collapsed to one entry on insertion. The Lua script's eviction then operates on this collapsed set, and the Python `_load_segment_data` will only see one copy. This is the same potential bug `sadd` had (it also dedups by member), but it is now more consequential because the score-based eviction changes ordering. Worth either documenting the assumption (that payloads are unique) or de-duplicating earlier so that eviction counts are meaningful.

ZUNIONSTORE used with destination equal to one of its source keys

`redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and the analogous `set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key` pass `set_key` as both destination and source. While this happens to behave correctly in some single-instance Redis versions (because the source data is gathered before the destination is rewritten), it is not documented as a supported pattern, can produce non-deterministic results across versions, and is a footgun in cluster mode where slot routing must already match. The safer equivalent is: gather members via ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE, then ZADD them to `set_key` (or union into a temp key and RENAME). At minimum this should be commented and pinned against a tested Redis version.

Admin-only pagination branch wraps a broken paginator behind an undocumented query flag

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` enables `OptimizedCursorPaginator` for superusers/org members with global access. Because the paginator's only distinguishing behavior (negative offsets) crashes Django (see paginator.py finding), the branch serves no purpose other than to expose a new failure mode. There is no test in this PR for the new branch, no documentation/changelog entry, and no consumer that actually needs negative offsets. This is dead/unsafe code shipped under an unrelated PR title; it should be reverted from this PR and either fixed properly or removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python hash() of a tuple of ints

The cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids))). While CPython's hash of a tuple of ints is deterministic within a given run, the contract relies on an internal implementation detail (the tuple hashing algorithm for nested ints) and produces a signed Python int that is concatenated into the key string. It would be safer and more portable to use an explicit deterministic digest (e.g. hashlib.md5 of the comma-joined sorted ids) so the cache key is stable across Python versions, implementations, and obvious to readers, and so cache busting via invalidate_upsampling_cache is reliable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the use of hash() in the cache key and recommend a deterministic digest so that invalidate_upsampling_cache works reliably. The candidate's rationale differs: it cites portability across Python versions and implementations, not per-process hash randomization. Since ints are not randomized in CPython, the candidate's reasoning is arguably more accurate. Still, it targets the same code issue with the same fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Aliased count() columns silently bypass upsampling transform

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling matches column_lower == "count()" exactly. Any column with an explicit alias such as "count() as my_count" or even "count() as count" will not match and falls through to the else branch, which appends the original column unchanged. The endpoint code (organization_events_stats.py) now calls this transform on every y-axis column when upsampling is enabled, so a user who aliases their count column (e.g. for a chart with multiple y-axes) will silently get the raw count() while a user with no alias gets the upsampled value. The fix is to detect count() with optional "as <alias>" and replace the function name while preserving the alias, e.g. emit "upsampled_count() as my_count".

topEvents error message changed, breaking API contract

The 400 response for topEvents <= 0 was changed from {"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"} to {"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}. This is a user-visible API contract change. Any client or integration that matches the previous string (e.g. Sentry's own frontend, alert rules, or downstream tooling) will stop recognizing the error. Either keep the original wording or coordinate this with the frontend before merging.

Tests mock options.get but do not clear the 60s upsampling cache

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (error_upsampling.py) caches the boolean result of the allowlist check for 60 seconds using cache.get/set. The four new tests in test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects etc. patch sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options, but if any earlier test in the same run (or a prior test in this class) has populated the cache for the same organization+projects, the cached True/False is returned without re-running options.get and the mock has no effect. This can cause intermittent failures or false successes. The tests should reset the cache (e.g. via cache.clear() or invalidate_upsampling_cache) in setUp/tearDown before patching options.

upsampled_count assumes sample_weight is non-NULL for every row

The new upsampled_count SnQL aggregate is implemented as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). SQL/ClickHouse sum() ignores NULL values entirely, so any event in an allowlisted project that lacks sample_weight (e.g. older data, a partial backfill, or a schema mismatch) will be silently dropped from the count. The comment in error_upsampling.py asserts the column exists for all events, but nothing verifies it at query time, and the consequence is wrong downsampled charts that look valid. The aggregate should either coalesce NULLs (assume a weight of 1 for rows without sample_weight, or surface a null result) or the allowlist check should validate that backfill has actually completed.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling mutates all event types, not just errors

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling is invoked unconditionally inside store_event right after manager.get_data() for every event, and writes normalized_data["sample_rate"] whenever contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate is present. The function does not check the event type, so any transaction, attachment, or other non-error event that happens to carry an error_sampling context (whether by a SDK bug, a test fixture, or a future feature) will have sample_rate injected, potentially affecting other code paths that read sample_rate from those events. Guard the call on the event type being an error, or move the logic into the error-specific normalization path.

Bare except Exception hides AttributeError/TypeError in sample rate extraction

In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling the first try/except wraps a chain of .get() calls on dicts, which never raise. The except Exception block is dead for the intended path but will silently swallow AttributeError or TypeError caused by a malformed normalized_data (e.g. contexts not being a dict). That makes a broken event manifest look like "no sample rate" instead of failing the test loudly. Catch only the specific exception you expect, or drop the try/except entirely around the .get() chain.

invalidate_upsampling_cache has no test coverage

invalidate_upsampling_cache is a public helper intended to be called when the allowlist changes, but no test in test_error_upsampling.py exercises it. Without a test, a future change to the cache key format (e.g. switching away from hash()) will silently break cache invalidation in production. Add a test that populates the cache, calls invalidate_upsampling_cache, and asserts cache.get returns None.

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is not exercised

The main public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects (which combines the allowlist check, the 60s cache, and the dataset/query filter) is never tested directly. The test file only covers the private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling). The caching behavior in particular is the riskiest new logic and should have a test that verifies a cache hit short-circuits the allowlist lookup.

Inside _get_event_stats, should_upsample = is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...) is immediately followed by upsampling_enabled = should_upsample and the rest of the function only ever reads upsampling_enabled. The second variable adds no semantic value and makes the code look like the two could diverge. Drop one (preferably upsampling_enabled) and use should_upsample directly. (Noted as style rather than bug because there is no functional impact.)

false_positives.candidate:
Stale denial cache can block legitimate access for up to 30s after a permission grant

The newly introduced permDenialCache is consulted at the very start of Service.Check (lines 116-121) and short-circuits to Allowed=false before the permCache or the database are touched. There is no invalidation tied to permission changes (grants, role/team membership changes, deletions). Once any (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) tuple has produced a deny response, that deny is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) and will be returned for every subsequent request, even if the underlying database now grants the permission. This is a regression introduced by the PR and works against its stated goal of letting users access newly created resources: any prior deny that happened to land in the cache for the same (name, parent) tuple will hold the new permission back for up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry whenever a permission grant or revocation affects the cached tuple, or use a much shorter TTL so the cache behaves as a brief burst guard rather than a 30s negative answer.

No test covers a stale denial cache blocking access after a permission grant

The denial cache can hold a deny entry for up to 30s after a user was last denied for a (name, parent, action) tuple. There is no test that asserts (and therefore no guard against) the regression scenario: a prior deny is cached for the user, but the underlying store now grants the permission, and Service.Check still returns Allowed=false because the denial cache short-circuits before the new fallback-to-DB path. Adding such a test would either confirm the 30s window is acceptable, or catch it if invalidation is later added.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The newly added `enableSqlExpressions` function reads:

```go
func enableSqlExpressions(h *ExpressionQueryReader) bool {
    enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)
    if enabled {
        return false
    }
    return false
}
```

The function unconditionally returns `false` regardless of the feature flag's state. The `enabled` variable and the `if enabled { return false }` branch are dead code (both branches return `false`). This is confusing because:
1. The function name suggests it checks whether SQL expressions should be enabled.
2. A future maintainer is likely to interpret this as buggy logic and "fix" it (e.g. by returning `enabled` or `!enabled`), which could accidentally re-enable the vulnerable code path.
3. The `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` check is functionally meaningless.

For a security hardening PR, the intent should be expressed unambiguously. Either simplify to `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or rename and invert the logic so the dead branches are removed.

The feature is not merely unimplemented; it has been intentionally disabled to mitigate CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI). A user reading the error or a downstream log/alert may conclude the feature was forgotten rather than turned off for security reasons. The message should clearly state that the feature is disabled (e.g. reference the CVE / security release) so that operators and users understand why a previously working dashboard now errors.

At minimum a test exercising `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `QueryTypeSQL` and asserting the new error should be added; ideally also a test covering `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` to confirm the in-memory DB stub returns the expected errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent callers will redundantly re-read the manifest

The function checks the cache under RLock, then re-acquires a write Lock to populate it. However, it does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write Lock. When N goroutines invoke GetWebAssets concurrently while the cache is still nil (typical at server startup), every one of them passes the RLock check, then takes the write Lock sequentially, and each independently reads `assets-manifest.json` from disk and overwrites the global. The expensive I/O — the very reason the cache exists — is repeated N times. After `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` (line 48) and before the `cdn := ""` line, add `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` to make this a correct double-checked locking pattern. Without it, the race detector is silenced but the cache offers no benefit under cold-cache concurrency.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem in GetWebAssets: the double-checked locking is incomplete because the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is overwritten with nil on read error, defeating caching for subsequent calls

On line 69 the code unconditionally assigns `entryPointAssetsCache = result` and on line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err`. If `readWebAssetsFromFile` returns an error (network blip, transient I/O failure), `result` is nil and the global cache is overwritten with nil. Because the write Lock is held, every concurrent caller will observe the cleared cache and will each attempt the file read again; any previously cached value is permanently lost even if it was still valid. The assignment should only happen on success, e.g. `if err == nil { entryPointAssetsCache = result }` before the return. (Note: this behavior pre-existed, but the PR is the natural place to fix it now that the variable is properly guarded.)
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug. The cache is unconditionally assigned the fetch result on line 69, so when the fetch fails, nil overwrites a previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

This PR explicitly fixes a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, yet no test file is added or modified. There is no existing concurrent test for GetWebAssets that would have caught the original race, and nothing here guards against reintroducing the same race (e.g. by removing the mutex or by reverting to the unlocked read in a future refactor). A short test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines in parallel and runs under `go test -race` would lock the fix in place and exercise the double-checked locking pattern described above.

Return statement is redundant and obscures intent

Line 70 returns `entryPointAssetsCache, err` after having just assigned `entryPointAssetsCache = result` on line 69. Both expressions yield the same pointer, but reading the code one must verify that no other goroutine could have changed the global between the assignment and the return. While holding the write Lock this is safe, but the redundancy invites future bugs (e.g. someone removing the mutex thinking the local `result` is the returned value). Simply `return result, err` is clearer and removes the indirection.

`r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...)` is emitted on every successful orphan-tag cleanup batch. This is a normal success log, not an error. Downgrade to `Info`/`Debug` and drop the always-nil `"err", y` field.

O(n²) string concatenation when building the SQLite inline IN-list

When `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit`, the code builds the IN-list with `values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0]); for _, v := range ids[1:] { values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) }`. Each `fmt.Sprintf` call copies the entire accumulator, so the total work is O(n²). With the newly added test case using a batch size of 32767, this is roughly a billion operations and ~hundreds of MB of garbage per cleanup batch, and it gets worse for any future larger batch sizes. The new and renamed tests (`TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp`, `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst`) only exercise SQLite via `db.InitTestDB(t)`. Without a MySQL integration test, a future regression in the locking pattern (e.g., re-introducing a subquery-based DELETE inside one transaction) would not be caught. The PR should include (or rely on an existing) MySQL integration test exercising concurrent inserts and the cleanup loop.

The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` uses `const sqliteParameterLimit = 999`. false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are no longer excluded from splitting

The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` runs before the `partition(... , query => !querySupportsSplitting(query))` step. `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep queries that contain `$__range` out of the time-split batches (the existing comment even explains that splitting such queries is incorrect because `$__range` would then be resolved against a sub-range). Because `applyTemplateVariables` resolves template variables and global variables (including `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__from`/`$__to`) on the frontend with the FULL time range, the `$__range` token disappears from `expr` before the check runs. The `isQueryWithRangeVariable` predicate then returns false and the query gets partitioned into `normalQueries` and split into 1-day chunks, each chunk receiving the full range baked into the previously-interpolated `$__range`. The result is wrong data: e.g. `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` over a 2-day dashboard range becomes `count_over_time({a="b"}[2d])` applied to a 1-day sub-range. The check needs to run on the original (pre-interpolation) expression, or `$__range` must be excluded from this frontend interpolation.

The comment in `querySupportsSplitting` says `$__range` is "interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange". After this PR the variable is interpolated on the frontend (`datasource.applyTemplateVariables`) with the full timeRange before the splitting decision, so the justification given in the comment no longer matches the code path. If the exclusion is still intended, the comment should be updated to describe the new ordering (check pre-interpolation expr, or skip `$__range` in the interpolation step); otherwise the check should be removed entirely.

Templates are interpolated once in runShardSplitQuery and again inside every nested runSplitQuery call

`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` on every non-hidden, non-empty target and passes the interpolated list to `splitQueriesByStreamShard`. Each shard group later builds a `subRequest` from these already-interpolated targets and calls `runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, ...)`. Inside `runSplitQuery`, the new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters))` re-runs template interpolation on the same queries. The test `'Interpolates queries before running'` codifies this by asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times for a single-target request (1 + 4 shard groups). Beyond the wasted work, if `applyTemplateVariables` is not strictly idempotent (e.g. it touches scopedVars, fires telemetry, mutates caches, or escalates unknown variables to errors) the second pass can change behavior or throw. Either `runSplitQuery` should be told the targets are already interpolated (skip flag / do not re-apply), or `runShardSplitQuery` should defer interpolation to the inner `runSplitQuery` call.

No regression test for $__range queries being excluded from splitting

The new `'Interpolates queries before execution'` test only covers `$__auto` and `$step` interpolation. Stray inside the group members table There is a stray closing tag inside the , sitting between and {{/each}}. A cannot be a direct child of a table outside cell context, so this is invalid HTML; browsers will attempt to repair the DOM, which can shift rendered elements and break the table styling that this PR is also touching. The tag is clearly leftover from an earlier template shape (the surrounding

add_members silently drops unknown or whitespace-padded usernames and still reports success

In the add_members action the usernames.split(",").each loop silently ignores names that don't resolve via User.find_by_username, and the split does no whitespace stripping, so an entry like " bob" (with a leading space) won't match the stored username and is also dropped. The action then renders success_json regardless of how many names were actually accepted, so the admin sees success even when every supplied username was invalid. Strip each username before lookup, and either reject the request or include the not-found names in the response so the caller can tell which entries failed.

add_members crashes with NoMethodError when usernames is sent as an array

params.require(:usernames) accepts whatever shape is sent; if a client posts usernames[]=alice&usernames[]=bob (the standard Rails array-param convention), params[:usernames] is an Array. The subsequent usernames.split(",") then raises NoMethodError because Array has no split method, returning a 500 to the caller. Coerce the param to a string before splitting (e.g. Array(params[:usernames]).flatten.join(",")) or return a 400 when the value is not a String.

The throw escapes the rejection handler and surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection, the bootbox alert is never shown, and the failure is invisible to the admin. Wrap the parse in a try/catch (or check that e.responseText is non-empty and parseable) and fall back to a generic message such as I18n.t('generic_error') when parsing fails.
