true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count and last_match_at are written twice per signup because validation runs twice

EmailValidator.validate_each delegates to `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which mutates the database (match_count, last_match_at). UsersController#create does `user.valid? && ... if user.save ...`, so the full validation suite — including this validator — runs once for the explicit `valid?` call and again when `save` re-runs validations. Each invocation of `should_block?` increments match_count by 1, so a single signup attempt with a blocked email inflates the counter by 2 (and any retry, double-click, or page-refresh multiplies it further). Make the validator purely read-only and push the statistics into an `after_validation` callback on User (gated by `email_changed?`), or detect a single increment via `update_all` and short-circuit the second call with an instance flag. Keeping validators free of side effects is the standard Rails contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the should_block check method has side effects: it updates match statistics during what should be a read-only check. The candidate focuses on a consequence of this (double counting during validation), but the underlying issue is the same, and it explicitly recommends keeping the check side-effect free. The golden comment also mentions race conditions, which the candidate does not.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive; case variants bypass the block

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive equality match, and the migration adds a case-sensitive unique index on the same column. User#email is not downcased on assignment, so a user registering as `Bad@Spam.com` will not match a blocked record stored as `bad@spam.com`, and admins can even create duplicate block rows with different casings. The whole purpose of the feature (stop spammers with known addresses) is defeated by trivial case mutation. Normalize on both sides: store the blocked email in a canonical (lower) form via a `before_validation` callback and add a unique index that ignores case (e.g., a functional index on `lower(email)` or a citext column), and compare with `where('lower(email) = ?', email.to_s.downcase)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the case-sensitive email lookup in the blocked email check, which lets a case variant of a blocked address get past the block.

false_positives.candidate:
rejectedEmails.contains compares strictly, so the user can bypass with a case change

In `emailValidation`, `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` is a strict equality check. The list is populated from `result.values.email`, which is whatever the server stored (case preserved). If the server previously rejected `Bad@Spam.com`, the user simply retypes `bad@spam.com` and the client-side check passes, even though the backend has the same case-sensitivity bug as `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. Lowercase both the stored and compared values (e.g., store `result.values.email.toLowerCase()` and compare `email.toLowerCase()` against the list) so client-side rejection matches the address the user is currently typing.

EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch; whitelist and blacklist are untested

EmailValidator#validate_each has three independent branches (whitelist, blacklist, BlockedEmail) but the spec only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts on the blocked-email path. There is no test that an email matching `email_domains_whitelist` passes, an email outside the whitelist fails with `user.email.not_allowed`, an email matching `email_domains_blacklist` fails, that the two settings do not interact unexpectedly when both are set, or that a nil/blank value is tolerated. Regressions in any of those branches — including the `elsif` ordering that means a non-empty whitelist silently disables the blacklist — will go undetected.

Spec asserts a single increment that production does not produce

The shared example `when a BlockedEmail record matches` calls `subject` once (which calls `should_block?` once) and asserts `match_count` changes by exactly 1. In production `should_block?` is invoked from `User#valid?` and again from `User#save`, so the same signup attempt actually increments by 2. The test passes because it bypasses the validator and exercises the model method directly, masking the doubled-write bug. Add a test that mirrors the controller path (build a User with a blocked email, call `valid?` then `save`, and assert the resulting `match_count`) so the inflated-count issue is caught at the spec level.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property -ms-align-items in align-items mixin

The generated rule `-ms-align-items: $alignment;` is not a valid CSS property. The correct IE10 flexbox prefix is `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted on the line above. `-ms-align-items` will be silently ignored by IE10 and IE11, providing no cross-browser benefit while bloating the compiled CSS. This is almost certainly a typo of `-ms-flex-align`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that -ms-align-items is not a valid property and that the correct legacy prefix is -ms-flex-align. The candidate identifies the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid CSS property -webkit-align-items in align-items mixin

The generated rule `-webkit-align-items: $alignment;` is not a valid CSS property and will be silently ignored by browsers. WebKit/Blink supports the unprefixed `align-items` property directly since Chrome 21 (no transitional `-webkit-align-items` was ever shipped). The 2009 flexbox variant `-webkit-box-align` is already included on the preceding line, so this line is redundant noise that bloats the output and signals the author misunderstood the prefix matrix.

Invalid CSS property -webkit-order in order mixin

The generated rule `-webkit-order: $val;` is not a valid CSS property. WebKit/Blink has supported the unprefixed `order` property since the 2012 flexbox spec shipped in Chrome 21; no `-webkit-order` transitional prefix was ever used in production browsers. The 2009-spec prefix `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` is already emitted above. This line is dead weight that ignores the actual prefix set and suggests the author did not verify the prefixed property names.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper has no effect — parent is not a flex container

`@include order(2)` is applied to `.extra-info-wrapper`, but its parent `#topic-title` (defined earlier in the same file) is not a flex container: `.title-wrapper` still uses `float: left; width: 90%;` and there is no `display: flex` (or `@include flexbox()`) on `#topic-title` or any of its ancestors in this stylesheet. The CSS `order` property only takes effect on flex items, so this call is effectively dead code and the intended reordering will not happen. Either the parent selector must be promoted to a flex container (and `.title-wrapper`'s float/width reverted) or the `order(2)` call should be removed.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name missing question mark — dead code

The new `include_website_name` method is defined without the trailing `?`. Throughout this file (and AMS conventions used by Discourse), every include predicate is named `include_<attr>?` (e.g., `include_email?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_stats?`). Without the `?` the serializer never calls this method, so it has no effect and `website_name` will be included in the JSON whenever its computed value is non-nil. It should be `def include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the main issue in the golden comment: include_website_name is missing its '?' suffix, so it is not used for conditional inclusion. It does not mention the secondary string-mutation point, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
TL0 users' website_name leaks to anonymous viewers

`:website` is registered with `untrusted_attributes`, which auto-generates `include_website?` to return `false` when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` (i.e., a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous/staff-with-restriction visitor). The new `include_website_name?` predicate (or the existing `include_website_name` if it's a typo) only checks `website.present?` and never calls `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. As a result, even when `website` is suppressed from the payload for a TL0 user, `website_name` (which still reveals the host and path the user has set) can still be serialized, bypassing the same privacy gate. Either add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` call (lines 105–111) or have the include predicate return `false if scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

website_name drops query string and fragment

`website_name` concatenates `URI(website).host` with `URI(website).path`, but never appends `.query` or `.fragment`. A user whose website is, e.g., `http://example.com/users/bob?tab=posts#about` will be displayed as `example.com/users/bob`, losing information the PR title advertises ('show complete URL path'). If the intent really is to mirror the original full URL when on the same domain, `URI(website).request_uri` (or host + path + query + fragment) should be used instead of just path.

No coverage that website_name is hidden from anonymous viewers of TL0 users

The 'with a TL0 user seen as anonymous' context asserts that `untrusted_attributes` (`:bio_raw`, `:bio_cooked`, `:bio_excerpt`, `:location`, `:website`, `:profile_background`, `:card_background`) are absent from `json`. After this change `:website_name` carries the same private information as `:website` and must be excluded by the same `restrict_user_fields?` gate, but the existing assertion was not extended and no new test exercises this case. Without such a test the privacy regression described above can be reintroduced unnoticed.

URI(website.to_s) parsed up to three times per call

`URI(website.to_s)` is invoked three times inside `website_name` (once for `.host`, then again for `.path` in each branch that includes the path). Each call constructs and parses a URI object. The value should be assigned to a local once (e.g., `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil`) and reused. The method is called for every user serialization, so this multiplies unnecessarily.

Drive-by doc comment change unrelated to PR

This PR is about changing the website display behaviour. The diff also edits the JSDoc above `profileBackground` from `@property websiteName` to `@property profileBackground` in `app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/user.js.es6`. The fix is correct, but it's an unrelated drive-by change that should be in its own commit/PR so the website-domain UX change stays focused and reviewable.

Subdomain check uses brittle two-segment suffix test

The `elsif` branch only fires when `discourse_host` and `website_host` have the same number of dot-separated segments and that count is `> 2`. A case such as `Discourse.current_hostname` returning `example.com` (2 segments) while `website_host` is `forums.example.com` (3 segments) skips the `elsif`, drops into `else`, and `discourse_host.ends_with?('.' + website_host)` is false, so the user sees just `forums.example.com` with no path even though the discourse host is a parent suffix of the website host. The condition that decides whether to show the path should be based purely on suffix relationship (e.g., one host ends with `.` + the other, or they are equal), not on equal segment counts, otherwise same-domain path display is missed in mixed-depth subdomain setups.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match, allowing spoofed origins

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any event whose origin contains `discourseUrl` as a substring. Anything like `https://attacker.com/?x=https://discourse.host`, or any subdomain/hostname that embeds the literal, passes the check, and the parent's height (or anything else e.data ever carries) can be set by an attacker frame. Because this same message handler also reads any e.data.type, a malicious frame could trigger other branches later. Use `new URL(discourseUrl).origin` (with a trailing slash check) and compare exactly: `new URL(e.origin).origin === expectedOrigin`.

The candidate's description of the substring direction is slightly off, since the code actually checks whether discourseUrl contains e.origin. That doesn't change the underlying issue, which is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Stored XSS: untrusted RSS content stored with raw_html cook_method

poll_feed reads `i.content` from the feed, runs only `CGI.unescapeHTML(...scrub)` (which strips invalid bytes but does not sanitize HTML), and passes it straight into `TopicEmbed.import`. import then creates a post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and, because Post#cook returns `raw` for that mode and best.html.erb renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, any `<script>` (or other active) tags in the feed end up executing inside an iframe whose origin is Discourse. The same vector exists for TopicEmbed.import_remote (Readability output is trusted and the raw URL body for Disqus) and the disqus.thor import. Anyone with admin control of feed_polling_url (or embeddable_host, or a Disqus import file) can get script execution in Discourse's origin and read cookies / take actions on behalf of logged-in users visiting the embed iframe. The fix is to never assign raw_html to imported posts from external sources; run them through the normal cook/sanitize pipeline.

New cook_method column default of 1 likely marks every existing post as raw_html

The migration adds `cook_method integer default 1 not null` to posts. Post.cook_methods is `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` and Post#cook short-circuits to `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. With conventional (0-indexed) Enum implementations `[:regular] == 0` and `[:raw_html] == 1`, so existing rows default to raw_html, which means Post#cook now returns the unprocessed markdown source. The before_save hook does `self.cooked = cook(raw, topic_id: topic_id) unless new_record?`, so the next edit on any existing post will overwrite `cooked` with raw markdown and visibly break rendering across the entire site. The migration default should be whichever value Enum maps to `:regular` (verify the Enum implementation; it is almost certainly 0, not 1).

embed/best does not validate that embed_url belongs to the embeddable host

`embed_url = params.require(:embed_url)` is used directly in `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and passed to `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, embed_url: embed_url)` without verifying its host equals `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The host check happens only asynchronously inside TopicRetriever. Anyone who knows an existing embed_url can render that topic via `/embed/best`, and any caller can enqueue a retrieve for a non-matching URL (it just silently no-ops in the retriever, but still hits the DB, the queue, and reveals embed existence). Validate the host synchronously in the controller before doing the lookup or enqueueing.

Imported posts created with skip_validations: true and raw_html can persist arbitrary content with no Sanitize pass

When `TopicEmbed.import` creates the initial post it passes `skip_validations: true` along with `cook_method: raw_html`. Combined, the post's `cooked` field stores whatever HTML the caller supplied, including `<script>`, `onerror=`, `<iframe>`, javascript: links, etc., and Post#cook then returns that raw content unmolested. Even though `absolutize_urls` runs on the content, it does not sanitize. Two follow-up problems: (1) the Disqus thor path later creates further reply posts via PostCreator without setting `cook_method`, mixing modes in the same topic; (2) `revisor.revise!(... , skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` overwrites the post with whatever the next import produces, also bypassed. Sanitize imported HTML before storing it and do not pair `skip_validations` with raw_html.

Synchronously executes the scheduled PollFeed job on every retrieve

`perform_retrieve` does `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inside the retriever job's execution. This pulls and parses the full RSS feed, hits RSS hosts, and writes TopicEmbeds for every item in the feed, all while the retriever itself (triggered by a user GET to /embed/best) is queued behind it. A large feed will make every embed request stall, and it ignores the PollFeed scheduling/throttling guarantees. The retrieve should only try to import the single embed_url, not rerun the whole feed poller inline.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Two `def self.downsize` definitions silently shadow each other

Any existing caller that previously invoked `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` will now dispatch to the new method, with the integer `max_width` being interpreted as a pre-formatted dimensions string and `max_height` being put inside the opts hash. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Client-side upload size check is hardcoded to 10MB and ignores site settings

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

Animated-GIF downsize path passes an invalid dimensions value to gifsicle

When SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is true, OptimizedImage.optimize routes through downsize_instructions_animated, which builds `gifsicle ... --resize-fit #{dimensions} ...`. The controller passes the literal string `"80%"` as dimensions, but gifsicle's `--resize-fit` flag expects pixel dimensions of the form `WxH`, not a percentage. true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. Passing '80%' to gifsicle --resize-fit in the animated GIF path fails, because the flag expects WxH geometry, so the downsize fails.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedImage.downsize is called with the same path for input and output

The auto-downsize loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...). The underlying convert (or gifsicle, for animated GIFs) command then opens the file for reading and writing at the same path. ImageMagick and gifsicle will truncate the destination before reading from it, which can produce an empty or corrupt output file. The next call to Upload.create_for will then persist a zero-byte or garbled image with no error surfaced to the caller or user.

413 entity-too-large error message hardcodes 10MB regardless of the real server limit

The case-413 branch now shows the user `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` irrespective of the actual server-side cap. When the server's effective limit differs from 10MB (because max_image_size_kb or the new download cap has been reconfigured), the error dialog misreports the threshold the user must satisfy. The user-facing message is now decoupled from the server's real limit.

URL download size cap is hardcoded to 10MB instead of using the site setting

FileHelper.download is now called with `10.megabytes` instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. The download cap is no longer configurable via the same knob as the rest of the upload flow, and any site whose configured `max_image_size_kb` differs from 10MB will see inconsistent behaviour between direct uploads and URL-sourced fetches. Given the new auto-downsize feature is supposed to let images larger than `max_image_size_kb` through, the download cap should be raised above that setting (or made explicit), not silently frozen at 10MB.

Auto-downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value and proceeds even on total failure

The while loop re-checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` but never inspects the boolean returned by OptimizedImage.downsize. OptimizedImage.convert_with rescues every error and returns false on failure (e.g., ImageMagick not installed, corrupt source), but the controller discards that signal and only decrements `attempt`. This controller fetches the row, mutates the attribute, and calls `save!`, so (a) no `MessageBus` event is fired (open clients keep showing the old level), (b) `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not refreshed, and (c) any race where the row is deleted between `find_by` and `save!` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. After mutating the notification level, the action falls through to `perform_show_response`, which renders the normal topic view. false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours comparison uses UTC time/day against organizer-local working hours

The working-hours guard compares `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())`, `slotStartTime.hour()` and `slotStartTime.minute()` against `workingHour.startTime/endTime`. `WorkingHours.startTime/endTime` are minutes since midnight and `days` is the organizer/day-local day-of-week (as produced by `getAggregateWorkingHours`/`getWorkingHours`), while `slotStartTime` was produced by `time.utc()`, so `.day()/.hour()/.minute()` are in UTC. The comparison only works when organizer TZ is UTC; for any other organizer timezone the day-of-week and time-of-day values do not line up and slots can be classified as in/out of hours purely based on the UTC clock. The slot must be converted to the organizer's timezone (or, in `checkIfIsAvailable`, to `organizerTimeZone`) before these comparisons.

Date-override day comparison formats in the server's local timezone

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats the shifted instant using the dayjs instance's default (server-local) timezone, not `organizerTimeZone`. The right-hand side `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is also in the server's local zone, so the two sides happen to match each other but not necessarily the organizer. When an organizer whose timezone is east of UTC enters an early-morning override (e.g. 06:30 IST = 01:00 UTC), `add(-330)` crosses midnight and the formatted day is the previous UTC day, so slots on the correct organizer day are rejected as outside the override. Use `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")` and `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")` to compare days in the organizer's timezone.

Multi-override semantics: first non-covering override incorrectly blocks the slot

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` loop returns the first override whose day matches and for which the slot is outside that override's range; the outer `if` then returns `false` (slot unavailable) regardless of whether another override for the same day does cover the slot. With several date overrides on the same day (e.g. 09-11 and 14-16), a slot at 09:30 is inside the first override but not the second, the find returns the second, and the slot is rejected. The semantic should be ANY (available if any override covers), not ALL. The simplest fix is to break out as soon as a covering override is found, and only return `false` if every override for that day fails to cover.

`dayjs.tz(date.start, override.timeZone)` used without guarding undefined

`override.timeZone` was just made optional on `TimeRange`, but `slots.ts` calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` unconditionally. `dayjs.tz(..., undefined)` does not throw on every code path but yields the host-local offset, which silently corrupts the offset math (`organizerUtcOffset`) and therefore every converted override time, producing wrong `startTime`/`endTime` minutes and wrong slots. Either require `timeZone` on the input, default it to `organizerTimeZone`/`timeZone`, or assert/throw when it is missing so the failure is not silent.

`const utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1;` followed by `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` is a non-standard way to express "view `date.start` in `organizerTimeZone`". It also relies on the offset at the exact instant `date.start`, so for multi-day date overrides that span a DST transition the start and end can be shifted by different amounts and the resulting window can be subtly incorrect. Replacing this with `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone)` (and equivalent on the slot) eliminates the manual offset handling.

The PR description and linked issues (#8207, #8329) state the change makes fixed hosts' date overrides count toward round-robin availability, but the new test only covers a single user with a date override at two different invitee timezones. There is no scenario that exercises a round-robin event with a fixed host plus a round-robin host where the fixed host has a date override restricting availability on a day; that is precisely the behaviour being fixed and currently has no regression test.

Use Prisma's atomic `increment` operation (e.g. `update({ where: { id }, data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } } })`) in both the `else` branch (line 179-186) and the `catch` branch (line 190-197).

This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

The new cleanup `deleteMany` uses an `OR` whose second branch is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch. The first branch is correctly scoped to SMS, but the second branch will delete any `WorkflowReminder` row (including EMAIL and WHATSAPP) whose `retryCount` exceeds 1, regardless of scheduledDate. Today only this SMS path increments `retryCount`, but any future change that bumps the counter for email/whatsapp (or a stray backfill) will silently delete those reminders too. The PR description's stated goal is to delete reminders that fail to schedule after two attempts, so empty message / missing recipient must also drive `retryCount` (e.g. increment in an `else` for the outer guard) or be deleted immediately.

The previously-public `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method has been deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions()`. The integration test now hard-codes a `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized"` query and the call sites have no documented API to add their own conditions.

Every assertion in the rewritten test compares the service output with a literal `Prisma.sql\`...\`` template using `expect(...).toEqual(...)`. `Prisma.Sql` is an object whose internal `strings` / `values` arrays are sensitive to whitespace, parenthesis placement, and the order of interpolation. The PR title and description say this only "updates the integration tests for the Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation", but the diff also substantially rewrites the service itself: deletes `findMany`, changes return types from `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` to `Prisma.Sql`, widens the constructor options type, removes the `NOTHING = { id: -1 }` sentinel, and adds `getBaseConditions()`. true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object URL for backup codes download is never revoked on unmount

A new object URL is created (line 99) and the previous one is revoked only when another URL is created (line 98). When the modal is closed or the component unmounts, the last backupCodesUrl is never revoked, leaking the underlying Blob for the lifetime of the page. Add a cleanup useEffect that calls URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) on unmount, and also revoke it in resetState() / when the user navigates away from DisplayBackupCodes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: the backup codes object URL is not revoked when the component unmounts, which leaks memory. The candidate adds more detail and suggested fixes, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
DisplayQrCode "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires handleEnable API call

The "Continue" button on the QR code step is rendered as type="submit" and lives inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209). Clicking it both runs the onClick (which advances to EnterTotpCode) AND submits the form, invoking handleEnable which immediately calls TwoFactorAuthAPI.enable() with whatever totpCode is currently in the form (empty or stale from a previous attempt). The result is a wasted API round-trip and an error toast like "code is incorrect" being briefly shown to the user before the step transitions. The button should be type="button" since its only intent is to advance the wizard step.

ConfirmPassword "Continue" button is type="submit" inside outer Form, fires two API calls

The ConfirmPassword Continue button is type="submit" and is placed inside the outer <Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}> (Form opens at line 209, the button is at line 233-240). Clicking it both runs the onClick handleSetup (which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup) and submits the outer form which calls handleEnable, which posts to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/enable. Because totpCode is empty at this point, the second call always fails and sets an error message in state, even on a successful setup. The button should be type="button" (or moved outside the outer Form) so that only handleSetup runs.

No rate limiting on 2FA disable endpoint, enabling brute-force of TOTP/backup code

The disable handler accepts a TOTP code (6 digits, ~20 bits of entropy) or a backup code (10 hex chars, 40 bits) and attempts verification on every request. Unlike the next-auth credentials authorize (which calls checkRateLimitAndThrowError), this endpoint performs no rate limiting, no lockout, and no failed-attempt counter. A user who is still logged in (or an attacker with a stolen session cookie) can submit unlimited guesses. TOTP is especially vulnerable: 10^6 / 30s is small enough that a targeted attacker can reliably find the current code. Add checkRateLimitAndThrowError (or equivalent) keyed on the user id before running code verification.

Returns 200 success without authenticating when 2FA is not enabled, leaking 2FA status

When user.twoFactorEnabled is false, the endpoint short-circuits with `return res.json({ message: "Two factor disabled" })` (line 37) without ever calling verifyPassword or checking the supplied code. Any caller who knows a valid session can use this to probe whether a given account has 2FA enabled: the response body and status differ from the "needs 2FA / needs password" branches. Either require the same authentication as the 2FA-enabled path before returning, or return a uniform response regardless of 2FA status.

Backup code authentication path is not exercised by any test

The e2e file has a TODO at line 12 ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and only verifies UI affordances (download/copy/close). The new security-critical paths added in this PR — backup-code login via next-auth-options.ts, backup-code disable via totp/disable.ts, single-use enforcement of backup codes, and the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes ErrorCode mappings in login.tsx — are not covered. Without these tests, regressions in single-use enforcement, race-condition fixes, or error mapping will go undetected. The author also explicitly ticked the checklist item "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works".

formatBackupCode referenced before declaration; download Blob built on first render

handleSetup (line 77) references formatBackupCode (line 163) inside its body. Because formatBackupCode is a const arrow function declared after handleSetup, this works only via closure hoisting at call time — easy to break by future refactors and confusing to read. More importantly, the Blob on line 95 is built using formatBackupCode but the downloaded file content can drift from what is shown on screen if the formatter changes between setup and download (e.g. different dash placement). Define formatBackupCode before handleSetup (module scope or above the component) so both the display grid (line 204) and the Blob/copy operations (lines 95, 278) use the same definition.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Calendar updateEvent passes undefined calendarId when no externalCalendarId is supplied

Inside `updateEvent` the new selection is `selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. The `find` callback compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, but the parent ternary only enters this branch when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (typically `undefined`), so `find` matches nothing and returns `undefined`. The previous code simply used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` and worked for any single-destination booking. As a result, callers like `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (which always omits `externalCalendarId`) now send `calendarId: undefined` to the Google Calendar API, causing the update to 404 even though the destination calendar is present on the event.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flawed find logic: comparing cal.externalId === externalCalendarId inside the ternary branch makes the lookup meaningless and always fail. The golden describes it as searching for a calendar that matches itself. The candidate correctly notes the else branch runs when externalCalendarId is falsy, so the find returns undefined. Same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty array on Meet bookings

The new fallback that decides whether to switch the meeting location to Cal Video no longer uses optional chaining. Line 119 destructures `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` into `mainHostDestinationCalendar`, and line 120 reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` directly. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`, `undefined`, or an empty array (a normal state for many bookings), the destructured variable is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`. The previous code (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`) safely evaluated to `true` in that case. Any booking whose `location` is Google Meet and that has no destinationCalendar configured will now crash with 500 instead of silently falling back to Cal Video.

Collective events silently drop all host destination calendars when organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is initialized as `null` when neither the event-type nor the organizer user has one (see the `evt = { ... destinationCalendar: ... ? [...] : null }` block around line 1067). The subsequent `if (isTeamEventType && eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE") { evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars); }` uses optional chaining, so the push becomes a no-op when the value is `null`. As a result, collective bookings that have no event-type-level or organizer-level destination calendar end up with an empty/null `destinationCalendar`, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` falls through to the `cred.type === "calendar"` branch which never matches real credentials (`google_calendar`, etc.). The expected per-host calendar invitations for that scenario are silently lost.

Only the first destination calendar of a collective booking is persisted on the Booking row

When writing the new booking row, the change connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` to the booking's `destinationCalendar` relation: `destinationCalendar: evt.destinationCalendar && evt.destinationCalendar.length > 0 ? { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } } : undefined`. For collective events the array now contains the organizer plus every host's destination calendar (built up by the `teamDestinationCalendars` push on line 1078), but the Booking schema only stores the first entry. Any later code path that consults `booking.destinationCalendar` directly (instead of `booking.references`, e.g. confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts at line ~251, paypal-webhook.ts line 152, deleteCredential.handler.ts line 290) will only see the organizer's calendar and lose information about the other hosts. This contradicts the PR description that the booking now supports multiple destinations per host.

Google Calendar deleteEvent always deletes from "primary" when externalCalendarId is omitted

`deleteEvent` uses the same `find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` lookup as `updateEvent`. With `externalCalendarId` undefined (the only form `CalendarManager.deleteEvent` ever calls it with), the lookup never matches and the fallback `calendarId: calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` resolves to `"primary"`. Previously it just used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Bookings whose host's destination calendar is not the user's Google primary calendar will now be deleted from the wrong calendar; for events that don't exist on primary, the 404/410 path silently resolves and the real calendar event is orphaned.

requestReschedule drops user fallback for destinationCalendar (inconsistent with other handlers)

The new assignment is `destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar] : []`. Every other handler in the PR (confirm.handler.ts:175, editLocation.handler.ts:85, handleCancelBooking.ts:251, deleteCredential.handler.ts:290, handleNewBooking.ts:1063) falls back to `user.destinationCalendar` when the booking has none. Here that fallback was removed (it was a typo'd duplicate in the old code), so reschedule webhooks and the reschedule email are now sent with `destinationCalendar: []` even when the booking's owner has a destination calendar configured. This is inconsistent and may mislead recipients about which calendar will be updated.

No test covers the core multi-host destinationCalendar fix

The PR author checked the box "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works." The only test change in the whole PR is updating the expected `destinationCalendar` value from `null` to `[]` in `apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts`. There is no integration or unit test exercising the new collective-event path: building the `evt.destinationCalendar` array with organizer + team host destinations, persisting it through `handleNewBooking`, or verifying that `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` fans out to all host calendars. Given the size of the refactor (signatures changed, persistence narrowed, multiple CalendarService adapters updated), this is a significant test gap and the regressions called out above (e.g. TypeError on Meet bookings, dropped team destinations, broken Google update/delete) are likely to pass through CI because nothing in the suite exercises the scenario.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) in requestReschedule drops calendar/video cleanup

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await its async callback, so the `await getCalendar(...)` + `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and the `deleteMeeting(...)` calls for each booking reference are started but never awaited. The function then proceeds to send the reschedule email/webhook and returns to the client, meaning external calendar events and video meetings from the original booking are not reliably cleaned up when a booking is rescheduled. This was an existing latent issue (deleteEvent was already async) but the conversion to async `getCalendar` makes the missing await even more important. Replace the forEach with a for-of loop or Promise.all so all cleanup promises are awaited before returning.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: forEach with async callbacks leaves the calendar and video deletion promises unawaited, so cleanup is unreliable. Both also recommend replacing it with for...of or Promise.all.

false_positives.candidate:
forEach(async) drops calendar cleanup on vital reschedule

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await its callback. The `await getCalendar(credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type))` and subsequent `calendar?.deleteEvent(bookingRef.uid, builder.calendarEvent)` invocations are untracked promises. The function returns `true` without waiting for these deletes, so a vital-related reschedule can complete without actually removing the previous calendar/video events on the external provider. The conversion from sync to async `getCalendar` makes this dependency concrete. Use `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... }` (with await inside) or wrap in `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

forEach(async) drops calendar cleanup on wipemycalother reschedule

Same pattern as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await its async callback, so the `await getCalendar(...)` + `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` calls run detached from the request lifecycle. The reschedule returns success without guaranteeing the prior calendar events are deleted. Use a sequential for-of or Promise.all to await the deletes before resolving.

getCalendarCredentials now returns Promise<Calendar> but types still say Calendar

`getCalendarCredentials` now constructs each `calendar` entry via `getCalendar(credential)`, which is async. The returned objects therefore have `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` at runtime, but there is no explicit return type or `.d.ts` update, so TypeScript still infers/asserts `calendar: Calendar | null`. This is an implicit API/contract break: any new or existing consumer that forgets to `await item.calendar` will call `.listCalendars()`/`.createEvent(...)`/`.deleteEvent(...)` on a Promise object and fail with a cryptic runtime error (e.g. `calendar.deleteEvent is not a function`). Either update the return type to reflect the Promise and rename the field (e.g. `calendarPromise`), or wrap the synchronous-style list construction with a single `Promise.all` inside `getCalendarCredentials` so callers see a real `Calendar` instance and existing call sites like `getConnectedCalendars` can drop their per-item await.

Calendar deletes serialized by for-of instead of Promise.all

The PR replaces the previous `forEach((credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(...)); })` with a sequential `for (const credential of calendarCredentials) { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); apiDeletes.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(...)); }`. This now awaits each `getCalendar` and each `deleteEvent` one credential at a time. For users connected to many calendars (or with `_other_calendar` integrations) this serializes what used to run in parallel and noticeably slows cancellation latency. Preserve the new await-semantics but parallelize with `const calendars = await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map(getCalendar)); apiDeletes.push(...calendars.map(c => c?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId)));` (or equivalent `.flatMap`).

Outer `calendar` variable unused after refactor

`const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential);` is now declared unconditionally but is only consumed in the `else` branch. In the `if (recurring && allRemainingBookings)` branch the code creates its own (shadowed) `calendar` inside the forEach callback, making the outer value dead. Either remove the outer declaration and move it into the `else` branch, or move the recurring-branch delete logic out so the outer calendar is actually used. As-is this is dead-await work and visual confusion about which calendar is being used.
